💡 Key Takeaways
  • Legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me.
  • A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards.
  • When I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me. As I crawled into position, a buck materialized in the scope. It had no idea I was there.

A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards. The evening air was dead calm.

When I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view. The shot was simple: one bullet from a Browning 6.8 Western dropped the deer, and my 2026 season was off to a good start.

Industry observers note that from the oak-studded knob on which I shot, I could see the North Umpqua River meandering through the valley below. It was on this river that I caught my first summer steelhead, at age 4, in 1968. In 1986 I shot my first wild turkey from the same area. That hunt sparked a 40-year passion chasing these grand birds.

Recent findings suggest that as I walked up on the high-racked buck, the river’s unique beauty was captivating. I wasn’t looking at just any whitetail, but a prized Columbia whitetail. Here we have the only huntable population of these special deer in the world. I was exactly one hour and 20 minutes from my home in Western Oregon.

Industry observers note that almost 50 years to the day prior, I shot my very first deer — a Columbia blacktail. That buck came less than 15 miles from my home. Over the decades I’ve shot some dandy blacktails and seen bigger ones that outsmarted me. I rank consistently killing a mature trophy Columbia blacktail as the most challenging of all big game hunting in North America. The habitat they call home is vast, varied and as dense as a tropical rainforest in places.

Less than a week after punching the whitetail tag I was in Oregon’s Coast Range. I saw seven bears in four days before shooting a mature, sleek-coated beauty. My wife and I love bear meat; she even renders the fat for cooking. It’s great this time of year.

Recent findings suggest that in the spring I hunted bears in the same area of the Coast Range. I passed 27 bears in seven days before pulling the trigger on a nice bruin.

In a recent development, earlier this month, friends and I got serious about duck hunting public land on nearby rivers, as we always do this time of year. The first two hunts found us targeting wood ducks. I shot seven-bird limits of the gorgeous little ducks each time out. The following trip was a mix of mallards and woodies, and after that, an all-mallard limit. Excellent eating, all of them.

One morning was extra special, as I achieved something I’d been trying to pull off for three seasons. The morning was foggy and wood ducks aggressively poured into the small spread of decoys. Shots were close. I took seven wood ducks along with a pair of honkers. While driving home with the double limit I got a text from a nearby landowner. A big flock of turkeys was back on his property. He asked if I’d come shoot some, as they were becoming a nuisance.

In recent years Oregon created a special hunt for problematic fall and winter turkeys. It’s called a beardless turkey permit and with it you can shoot three turkeys without visible beards, on each of the three available permits that are purchased over the counter. It’s a depredation hunt that was put in place to deter large flocks of fall turkeys from congregating on private property, causing damage and leaving messy gifts that are a health concern to pets and livestock. Since funding to trap and relocate turkeys was cut in the state, turkey numbers have exploded in many counties. It’s common to see multiple flocks a day of 100 or more turkeys, all fall and winter long, in several places around Oregon.

I hurried home, grabbed Echo, my pudelpointer, and headed out for the turkeys. Echo is almost 13 years old. She’s hunted fall turkeys every year of her life. Oregon is one of a handful of Western states that allows the use of dogs for fall turkey hunting. It’s one of my favorite hunts of the year and Echo loves it. For Kona, my 10-year-old male pudelpointer who I lost to an intestinal torsion this past September, this was his favorite hunt of all. It was hard heading afield without him, for the first time.

Industry observers note that but Echo didn’t skip a beat. After some searching we finally located the flock of turkeys. There were 46 of them, all hens, jakes, and jennies. They fed on the edge of a grassy meadow, heading uphill toward a patch of Douglas fir timber. When the time was right, I sent Echo. She ran at the flock as fast as her aging legs could carry her. She’d done this many times in her life. She knew the drill. If all the birds flushed, I’d call her back, we’d sneak into the timber, set up and call the flock back in. That didn’t happen.

Sources indicate that this time Echo caught the turkeys by surprise. A few flew into the trees but most burrowed into thick blackberries and tall, green ferns. Echo struck the perfect point and held it until I arrived. Turkeys often hold tight as quail. When I got to Echo, a jake made a run for it. It didn’t make it far. At the shot, the rest of the flock scurried, some running, some taking wing. I shot another bird on the run, then dropped one more from the air. Echo couldn’t gather them fast enough. Finally, my bird trifecta was completed.

We ate birds for dinner that night, and Tiffany whipped up multiple dishes for a big church potluck the following day. Everyone enjoyed the local bounty, and there was an extra sense of pride among the elderly men who used to hunt.

In a recent development, I’ve been fortunate to hunt much of the country, and even lived in Alaska for a stint in the 1990s. When it comes to hunting and fishing, I’ve found no other state that matches what Oregon has to offer. It boasts hunting opportunities for 12 significant game species, including four subspecies of deer. It has the best turkey hunting I’ve seen, with 14 tags available a year, including three spring toms. Thirty-three of the 41 recognized waterfowl species can be hunted here, along with bonus Eurasian wigeon which are becoming more frequent. Wigeon are my favorite duck to hunt and they thrive in the valleys and coast.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re into predator hunting, coyotes and bobcats abound statewide. Mountain lions are now classified as massive game in Oregon. In the past few years I’ve called in eight cougars, shooting the last one at 12 paces, using a shotgun. Last year I caught 11 different lions on trail cameras in one morning, all within 25 miles of my home–seven were within two miles. Cougars are thick, I wish we could hunt them with hounds as numbers are out of control. But some of our game laws make zero sense.

In a recent development, most recently Oregon made national news for the infamous Oregon Initiative Petition 28. IP 28 didn’t even appear on the November ’26 ballot. Yet, just about every blurb on the topic for the past year made it appear certain Oregon was going to lose all hunting and fishing privileges. Much of the press and pursuers of clickbait chastised Oregonians, ignorant of the full story and who the players were. In the fine print, IP 28 was absurd not only to hunters and anglers, but cattle ranchers, farmers, pet owners and more folks in our state.

According to recent reports, I was stunned at the number of fellow outdoorsmen who threw Oregon sportsmen under the bus, telling them to move from the state. Oregon is not the problem. Our matter is that the state is largely governed by people in three cities. The hunting and fishing population outside those city limits is large, and the many animals thriving in the game-rich state know no such boundaries nor are they aware of the people who set the rules. One hunting or fishing trip to our great state will reveal how special it truly is.

Sources indicate that for the past 26 years I’ve made a living as a full-time writer and wildlife photographer. For 14 of those years I hosted hunting and fishing TV reveals. I’ve written more than 4,200 magazine articles and 17 books with more in the works. I couldn’t have done it if not for living in Western Oregon, in the little town of Walterville — named after people on my wife’s side of the family.

Minutes from my home there’s something to hunt or fish for every day of the year. I live on the McKenzie River, a tributary of the famed Willamette River. I caught my first spring chinook salmon from the McKenzie in the 1960s. Over the decades, it, along with the Willamette River, have produced thousands of springers and loads of summer steelhead and rainbow trout for my family. Growing up fishing these rivers  spoiled me.

In a recent development, the Willamette River is big, wide, and challenging to fish in places. Downstream from where the Willamette flows into the mighty Columbia River, you’ll find some of the world’s best salmon and sturgeon fishing.

According to recent reports, the McKenzie River is a blue ribbon rated trout stream, one of the best in the country. Growing up, word traveled fast when movie stars were on the water, most presenting dry flies to try and entice stunning redsides.

Industry observers note that A few miles from my home, Theodore Roosevelt loved to fish for rainbow trout. I know where he stayed and the holes he liked to fish. Rumor has it–from some of my wife’s relatives who homesteaded the McKenzie River Valley in the mid-1800s–it was among Roosevelt’s favorite rivers to fish, both for the trout and the sheer beauty the region offered. Roosevelt would be happy to know that the place he so loved is now teeming with wildlife, including elk that carry his name.

According to recent reports, in fourth grade I began trapping. My parents took turns taking me to check traps before school. For sets close to home, I’d ride my bike. Beaver, raccoon, coyote, red fox and bobcat were some of the target species. I skinned the catch after school. This continued into my freshman year of high school, until sports consumed my life. Trapping greatly educated me about the land and the animals that live there. It also allowed me to make some money so I could fish in the summer months, rather than work.

In the 1970s, most duck hunting I experienced was on the rivers. In my formative years Dad, Grandpa and I spent many days together in duck and goose blinds.

According to recent reports, less than an hour from my home the first ring-necked pheasants were introduced to the continental United States. Birds arrived by sea in 1882, from China. Dad and grandpa shared many stories of incredible pheasant hunts they had in the 1950s and ‘60s. “Best pheasant hunting in the country,” Grandpa remarked. He wasn’t wrong. Today, we don’t pester what few pheasants remain in the valley. But parts of Eastern Oregon are flourishing with ring-necks. A few years back, Echo and I secured a limit of ducks, pheasants and valley quail on one of our best days, ever.

Valley quail and mountain quail thrive around my home. Getting on multiple coveys a day is common. The occasional ruffed grouse is put up in the valley, but they’re more prevalent in the foothills of the Cascades and Coast Range. Just above ruffed grouse in the mountains are blue grouse. When I was a kid we never saw a blue grouse below 2,000 feet. Today we shoot a lot of the substantial birds at and below 500 feet. More than once I’ve taken valley and mountain quail, blue and ruffed grouse on the same day. Truly special hunts, all of them.

Sources indicate that in mid-September band-tailed pigeons are the target. They occupy both mountain ranges and parts of the valley floor. In my days of youth the daily limit was seven, today it’s only two. Still, dogs love these hunts, as does my 86-year-old father. Intercepting speeding birds as they fly ridgelines in search of berries, minerals and water makes for challenging shooting and steep country retrieves.

It has been revealed that in the fall we chase Western gray squirrels. Kona loved treeing gray squirrels almost as much as he reveled in fall turkey hunting. The furry tree-dwellers are delicious.

For decades, cackling Canada geese have flocked to the Willamette Valley to graze on rye grass. The Willamette Valley is dubbed The Grass Seed Capital Of The World, and this prime food attracts loads of big game and waterfowl. Minimas — the smallest of the cackling Canada geese — regularly funnel into big decoy spreads in flocks of 10,000 or more. Words can’t be heard over the screaming little geese.

Thirty minutes from home, in multiple directions, is the best duck hunting I’ve found anywhere in the country. One day you’re hunting wigeon and pintails in flooded fields; the next, picking greenheads in tiny creeks surrounded by tall trees. You can regularly shoot a seven drake limit of wood ducks on public waters and private land filbert orchards, what outsiders call hazelnuts. The valleys hold some of the world’s best soil for filbert farming. As these orchards have expanded in recent years, wood duck and mallard numbers continue to grow because they love feasting on the nuts. Today there are more wood ducks than I ever recall seeing in my 51 years of hunting them.

It has been revealed that as I finalize these words, I’m preparing for the next several days afield, all near home. Tomorrow I’ll be hunting wood ducks on the river. The day after that, checking my 75 trail cameras set in the nearby hills. And the day after that I head to the Coast Range to hunt secretive Roosevelt elk in the rainforest. Last November I took a 340-class Roosevelt 35 minutes from home, my biggest Roosy bull to date.

There’s no better place to be, doing what I love the most. Oregon is a grand place to grow up, and to grow old.

Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Finally Resigns as Plea Deal in Elk Poaching Scandal Draws Hunter Outrage

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker.
  • It has been revealed that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov.
  • Industry observers note that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker. Harshbarger took a plea deal on Nov. 9 to dismiss five of seven charges related to illegally killing two bull elk in the region he represents.

It has been revealed that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov. Brad Little’s chief of staff, Zach Hauge, in response to Harshbarger’s resignation, obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little.”.

Industry observers note that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives. The former commissioner stepped away from commission duties once he was charged, but retained his seat until this week while the case continued, effectively leaving the position vacant.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, States He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

“I understand everyone deserves their day in court, but commissioners are charged with making and upholding our regulations,” Nick Fasciano, executive director of the Idaho Wildlife Federation, tells Outdoor Life. “And we do expect them to be held to a higher standard. The whole thing is disappointing.”.

The commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists. Each member of the commission can serve two four-year terms, and no more than four commissioners can come from the same political party. Harshbarger is a farmer in Ashton, Idaho. It’s an area known for massive chunks of public land and substantial grain and potato operations.

In a recent development, “I love our wildlife and the community we live in,” Harshbarger’s profile read on the commission’s website before it was removed. “We have a lot of challenges, and I am excited to help continue to solve them. What an amazing place to live and work.”.

According to recent reports, harshbarger pled guilty to hunting without a tag and shooting across a road. The remaining five charges, which are being dismissed in exchange for his guilty plea, are two illegal significant-game kills, hunting from a vehicle, failure to retrieve game, and trespass (one bull was on private property).

In a recent development, when news of Harshbarger’s plea deal went public, hunters and anglers started contacting regional IDFG offices and the governor’s office to demand his removal. The plea deal means his penalties could be as low as $500 and a one-year hunting suspension when he’s sentenced Dec. 9.

Frustration has also boiled over on social media around Harshbarger’s case.

Sources indicate that “Wake up Governor Little and do the right thing,” one Instagram user commented on the news of the plea deal, prior to Harshbarger’s resignation. “You and Senator Risch are already working to sell off our public lands and now you won’t step in to protect our wild game. Shame on you two.”.

Recent findings suggest that harshbarger was appointed by Gov. Little in 2024.

“Public trust is difficult to earn and easily lost,” wrote Idaho state Rep. David Leavitt in an email sent to Little on Tuesday that called for Harshbarger’s dismissal. “Maintaining that trust requires us to uphold the same principles regardless of who is involved. Idaho citizens deserve nothing less.”.

Recent findings suggest that little is also now in charge of appointing the director of IDFG. The commission did that until this year, when Little signed a publicly opposed bill into law changing the procedure from a seven-person decision to a one-person appointment by the governor, with confirmation by the state Senate.

Recent findings suggest that “Commissioners and the director now serve at the pleasure of the governor,” Fasciano says. “The commission is not empowered to boot out one of their own members even if they were so inclined.”.

Current IDFG director Jim Fredericks, a career fisheries biologist, was already leading the agency when the newly introduced law took effect July 1, making him the state’s last director selected by the commission.

Recent findings suggest that “The actual department of Fish and Game is going to take some heat for this [Harshbarger incident], but they weren’t the decision makers here,” Fasciano says. “The commission and the director were not able to drive a resolution here and they are also not responsible for the sentencing. A lot of frustration is going to be directed toward them, that isn’t their fault.”.

#67884. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2458 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The significant whitetail buck and I badly startled each other.
  • After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding.
  • It has been revealed that but then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The significant whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

It has been revealed that but then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

Sources indicate that that’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

Sources indicate that very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

It has been revealed that the stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

It has been revealed that slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too quickly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

Sources indicate that the real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

Industry observers note that don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

Recent findings suggest that A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

Don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

Recent findings suggest that once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

After searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is notable. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Sources indicate that want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Recent findings suggest that massive or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

It has been revealed that if you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

Sources indicate that often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as new snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

The lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, newly introduced to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

Sources indicate that the inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

Some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

Where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

Best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

In a recent development, worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

Some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

Snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles quickly with a few hours of sun.

According to recent reports, the stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

Industry observers note that of course, game does move out of high country when major snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

Gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

It has been revealed that harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

Industry observers note that clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

For quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

It has been revealed that pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”.

“Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”.

It has been revealed that A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

Recent findings suggest that this story, “Deer on the Prowl,” appeared in the January 1990 concern of Outdoor Life. Read more from this series:.

The Pentagon Wants Public Lands ‘Offered Up’ for a New Army Base. Wyoming Is Interested

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a upcoming military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.
  • The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest.
  • Hegseth said the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a upcoming military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

Hegseth said the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”.

But much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path currently exists for how to requisition and build a new military installation on federal public land, mentioned Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

The Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management aims that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

It’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet notes all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

Industry observers note that wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

The DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management initiative, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

“A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace indicates, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Ultimately, however, Squillace claims any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

Review: Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX Winter Hiking Boots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a newly introduced waterproof and insulated hiking boot from Oboz, known for its popular 400g Bridger 10″ and 200g Bridger 8″ insulated mid winter hiking boots.
  • If you’re a hiker, but you don’t hike in winter, you’re missing out on a lot of fun.
  • Several companies, including La Sportiva, Hoka, and Salomon, have attempted to introduce lightweight mids and trail runners for winter use with mixed success, because there are so many different types of winter hiking outings, from trail running and snowshoeing to light mountaineering, all targeting different user types, temperature ranges, complementary gear types, and trail conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a newly introduced waterproof and insulated hiking boot from Oboz, known for its popular 400g Bridger 10″ and 200g Bridger 8″ insulated mid winter hiking boots. Modeled after cross-country ski boots, the Katabatic Storm GTX is a lightly insulated mid-height boot insulated with aerogel-based Solarcore bonded to a Gore-Tex liner, providing waterproofing and warmth without added bulk. The result is an active winter boot with about 80% of the warmth of Oboz 200g insulated Bridger boots, that’s robust enough for use with lite traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons.

If you’re a hiker, but you don’t hike in winter, you’re missing out on a lot of fun. Gone are the bugs, roots, and rocks that can make three-season hiking unpleasant. The trails are less crowded, and there are lots of newly introduced skills to learn and gear to play with. In the past 15 years, winter footwear has gotten lighter and lighter due to advances in insulation technology, material science, and manufacturing practices. The introduction of lightweight traction aids, like microspikes, was a real inflection point because they could be used with footwear that has lightweight, flexible soles, requiring no special training like rigid mountaineering boots and crampons.

Several companies, including La Sportiva, Hoka, and Salomon, have attempted to introduce lightweight mids and trail runners for winter use with mixed success, because there are so many different types of winter hiking outings, from trail running and snowshoeing to light mountaineering, all targeting different user types, temperature ranges, complementary gear types, and trail conditions.

With that in mind, the Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a winter hiking boot, not a trail-running shoe, because its sole is too rigid. It is lightly insulated, with about 80% of the insulation of a 200g Thinsulate boot, and is good for temperatures down to about 15 degrees as long as you are moving and not standing still. It has enough front toe-kick rigidity to work with traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons without causing friction on top of the toes, which can lead to blisters or cold toes because of reduced circulation. The boots have a gaiter hook, making the boots compatible with gaiters. The outsole has lugs that provide good traction on snow and frozen slush when you’re not wearing a traction aid.

Sources indicate that fitwise, the Katabatic Storm is true to size. That stated, they’re patterned on cross-country ski boots, with a quick-lace system and a zippered top cover, which makes them a little time-consuming to put on and hard to adjust if you use an articulated lacing technique that requires different pressure at different points along the lacing track. I’m not a huge fan of either, but they fit me well enough, hold my foot securely, and don’t cause any hot spots inside.

I was a little leery of the Katabatic Storm GTX when I learned they only have a warmth value of about 80% of a 200g insulated winter hiking boot. The insulation they do have is only located in targeted areas such as underfoot, over the toe, and through the tongue, but not along the sides and around the heel. The shoe is designed for movement and managing the heat it generates, but not for standing around.

Why would that be an concern? As a winter hiker, I generally recommend buying insulated boots that will keep your feet warm when you’re not moving and are standing still. This is especially true if you hike in the backcountry where you may have to wait a long time, say 8 hours or more, for search and rescue to come and help your injured hiking partner while you wait with them, or if you have to slowly walk an injured hiker out into the wee hours of the morning. That’s not the time to wear a lightly insulated boot designed only for movement. That might sound overly conservative, but I have participated in backcountry winter rescues that ran into the early hours of the following day, and we were all very glad we were wearing heavily insulated boots.

It has been revealed that the insulated Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX boot is lightweight and comfortable, even on challenging hikes that require traction. I just wish they were available with more insulation that’s equivalent to the 400g Oboz 10″ Bridger insulated winter hiking boots I wear today. If they were, I’d wear them on every winter hike. As such, they’re ideal for shoulder season weather and spring conditions where there’s ice and slush on trails, but temperatures are warmer during the day. Because they are only lightly insulated, I reserve them for winter hikes on warmer days and close to accessible trailheads where local SAR crews can muster and arrive relatively swiftly in an emergency.

Disclaimer: Oboz donated boots for review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure. There are about 25 parks in the popular program, with two firearms hunts allowed on most of them. Each hunt runs just two days.

“I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life. “Trail cameras are not allowed on park [land]. But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”.

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

Sources indicate that “It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” indicates Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”.

Recent findings suggest that as the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy demonstrated me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”.

Sources indicate that on the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a big walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

“I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he indicates. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”.

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

“I started shaking, and yelling,” he says. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I noted yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”.

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

In a recent development, “I was in complete shock,” he indicates. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”.

It has been revealed that he filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

The buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

Recent findings suggest that he will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

It has been revealed that “The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” says Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

I Went Duck Hunting During the Infamous Armistice Day Storm, and Lived to Tell About It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.
  • In a recent development, it started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 issue of Outdoor Life.

There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.

In a recent development, it started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60. Fellows went duck hunting in shirt sleeves. The wind picked up velocity as the day went along, but not enough to get excited about — not until late afternoon. Then, with little warning, a full-scale prairie blizzard screamed in out of the northwest.

By dark the air was smoking with gale-driven snow, and the thermometer plunged near zero. Bitter winds blew all night. The weather experts remarked afterward that gusts hit 80 miles an hour. The storm laid a track of death and destruction across six states; it pounded ships to pieces on the Great Lakes, blocked roads, isolated towns, paralyzed cities, and buried cars. Hundreds were marooned on highways. A crack streamliner was 27 hours late into Minneapolis. And when the morning of November 12 broke, 20 duck hunters lay dead, frozen in stiff, grotesque poses — scattered on mud bars, sand spits, and willow-grown islands of the Mississippi bottoms between Red Wing, Minnesota, and La Crosse, Wisconsin.

I was among the luckier ones. I spent that terrible night with two companions under an overturned skiff on a mud bar — wet from head to foot, without fire or heavy clothing, pants frozen to my legs, and kept alive only by the body warmth of the men who lay huddled on both sides of me. The storm cost me six weeks of agony in a hospital and half of my left foot. But at least I survived.

Sources indicate that I was 14 at the time, attending high school in my home town of Winona, Minnesota. We got out of classes at 11 o’clock because it was Armistice Day. I scurried for home, planning an afternoon of duck hunting.

Sources indicate that the wind was already fairly fresh and mother was uneasy. “The storm warnings are up,” she told me while getting my lunch. But I grew up in Winona and knew the river, and at that age, bad weather didn’t worry me. The only thing it meant to me was good shooting. Ducks had been scarce all fall and maybe a blow would bring ’em down. So I hurried through lunch, impatient to get in a blind.

While I was loading my gear in the car, my cousin, Bob Stephens, showed up with a partner, Cal Wieczorek, and they decided to join me. Bob was 20, Cal about 19.

We drove to the Prairie Island spillway at the lower end of the Winona pool, where Dad kept his boat. It was a 16-footer, pointed at both ends, with a homemade bracket for an outboard. We decided to hunt a place known as the Firing Line, along the border of the Upper Mississippi Wildlife Refuge, three or four miles upstream. Hunters lined up there to intercept ducks flying in and out of the refuge. In stormy weather the pass-shooting was exceptionally good, and this looked like that kind of day.

Recent findings suggest that the wind was blowing half a gale now and was beginning to bite. Ominous dark clouds raced overhead, and scuds of cold rain pelted down as we clamped our old three-horse outboard on the boat, cranked it up, and headed out into the choppy pool. The three of us were a heavy load, and the skiff made slow headway against the wind.

We didn’t give it a thought then, but we couldn’t have been more poorly prepared. I was wearing cotton clothes — pants, shirt, socks, and a jacket lighter than a hunting coat. I had overshoes over my leather shoes. Bob and Cal were dressed similarly, except for hip boots. Cal and I had gloves. Bob had a heavy raincoat, and I still believe that made the difference between living and dying for me.

Sources indicate that we had one book of matches and no pocketknife. I was carrying a 16 gauge single-barrel Winchester; the other two had pumps. Because we intended to pass-shoot, we took no decoys.

Recent findings suggest that backed up by a series of low dams, the Mississippi is two to three miles wide in that section, flooding its bottoms and forming open lakes, meandering channels, small islands, bars, and rush beds. We threaded our way through this maze, wallowing in the heavy seas. It took us 1½ hours to cover the distance to the Firing Line.

The sky was full of ducks; they were barreling across the bottoms in crazy skeins, riding the wind, and turning and twisting below treetop height. It was plain they didn’t like the weather. Before the afternoon was over I actually swung at a greenhead with my gun as he hovered above my head, almost stationary, while bucking the gale.

Sources indicate that when we finally got to the Firing Line it was too crowded. The blinds were only about 25 yards apart and all occupied. Ducks were rocketing back and forth over the marsh and there was a steady barrage of shooting. We decided to find another spot.

By the time we found it — on a willow-covered island with many rushes in front — we were beginning to lose interest. The wind was howling like a banshee, down off the high bluffs to the west, with sleet and fine snow in its teeth. We hunkered in the willows for almost an hour, killed four ducks, and decided we’d had enough. The cold was already bone-chilling, our hands were so stiff we could hardly handle our guns, and we were starting to worry about getting back to the landing.

Sources indicate that two strangers came by in a little duck boat; they told us they were scared. That settled it for us, but going home was easier mentioned than done. None of us knew exactly where we were, and when we tried to shove away from shore, the seas threatened to swamp us. We finally dragged the skiff to the lee side and managed to get it afloat and start the motor. But before going 200 yards we ran aground on a mud bar, which we couldn’t skirt because of the wind and seas. We dragged the boat across the bar and started on again.

We did that about four times before finding ourselves by a substantial open slough and admitting we were lost. It was almost dark now and snowing so hard we couldn’t see 100 feet. We couldn’t even look into the wind — the storm cut our eyeballs like a sandblast. And the slough was a welter of dirty foaming water in which our skiff probably wouldn’t last more than a minute.

Industry observers note that while we debated what to do, another boat loomed out of the stormy dusk, riding low with four hunters. Two of them were only a little older than I — one from my home room at school. The others were men who had hunted the river bottoms all their lives. When they mentioned they knew the way to Prairie Island and could make it without swamping, we decided to follow.

In a recent development, but I couldn’t get the outboard started. Bob and Cal rowed, handicapped by cold-numbed hands, while I tinkered with it. We managed to keep the other boat in sight for a few minutes. Then, pitching and rolling, it disappeared and we didn’t see it again. When our frantic yells brought no answer we realized we were again on our own. It was days before we learned what happened to the other party. Their skiff had capsized when we lost sight of it. Three of the hunters died there, standing in the icy water, not knowing which way to go to dry land. By some miracle one of the boys survived the night and rescue parties found him on a near-by island at daybreak.

It has been revealed that only a few minutes after we lost that boat we were washed ashore on a sand spit. Bob and Cal leaped clear as we grounded and escaped a wetting. I was in the stern of the skiff, working on the outboard — right in the path of a wicked sea that smashed over us the instant we touched bottom.

I can’t describe the shock that icy dunking gave me. I clawed my way out of the swamped boat, and the wind cut like a braided whip. My legs wouldn’t hold me up, so I crawled across the mud until I was beyond reach of the waves and lay there, cold and weak.

Cal and Bob dragged the boat up on dry land, turned it over, and propped one side up to make a shelter. When they finished I crawled under it. My pants and jacket crackled as I moved. They had frozen stiff in the few minutes I lay exposed to the wind.

Sources indicate that we still had only a vague idea of our location, but we knew that large open lake, which we couldn’t cross in our puny skiff, lay between us and any landing. We didn’t talk much about it; we didn’t need to. Live or die, we’d have to spend the night where we were.

It has been revealed that bob and Cal did everything possible. They gathered rushes and put them under the boat to keep me off the wet mud. Then they searched desperately for firewood, but there wasn’t so much as a scrub willow. They finally found a few pieces of water-logged driftwood, heaped them in a pyramid, and turned the outboard motor up to drain gas on it — a risky thing to do, except in a desperate emergency like ours. But the screaming wind whipped the gas into nowhere as fast as it ran out of the tank. They struck one match after another without getting a spark of fire.

It has been revealed that the last match flared and died in the darkness, and they crawled under the boat and lay down on the wet rushes, one on each side of me. They spread their hunting coats over us and laid Bob’s raincoat on top. The raincoat kept the worst of the wind out and probably saved me from freezing.

We had little sense of time and hardly talked. Bob told me afterward that I spoke only two or three times during the night, and then I worried about the anxiety my parents must be feeling.

Sources indicate that I shivered for what seemed like hours, with my hands wedged between my thighs, since that seemed to be the warmest place on my body. I prayed silently. I didn’t think much about dying. I believed we’d get through the night somehow and in the morning find our way home. I realized finally that all feeling was gone in my feet; they were wooden stumps, no longer a part of me. I must have dozed, for I recall waking up and feeling warm, but that lasted only a minute or two and then I was shivering again.

It has been revealed that the thing I remember best was the unending scream of the wind. It never stopped raging — searching under the overturned boat, wailing, screeching, terribly alive, terribly cold.

In a recent development, sometime in the night Bob remembered that he had two apples and two sandwiches in his hunting coat. They were frozen hard, but we gnawed at them and they seemed to help.

The sound of distant gunshots reached us several times, and once we thought we heard faint, far-off yells for help. But our own guns were so crusted with ice that we couldn’t fire them, and it was useless to shout.

Sources indicate that we knew we weren’t the only hunters lost on the river bottom. Others were enduring the same torture. And we felt sure there must be rescue parties trying to find us, but we didn’t think we could count on them while the storm continued.

It was days before we learned all that happened that hard night. Rescue efforts began at dark, and men fought the storm and seas all night in skiffs and powerboats. Some even waded the sloughs to bring lost men to shore. It wasn’t a night for small craft, and no one will ever know how many boats were overturned, swamped, and driven back. But the search went on, hour after hour, heedless of the wind, cold, and snow.

Industry observers note that the night was an awful ordeal for the hunters. One party huddled on a marshy island beside a fire started with dead grass and fed with more than 40 cedar decoys. Gas from an outboard was used to rekindle the blaze each time it died down. Another group marched, jumped, and sparred around a fire built from their boats. Still another found a patch of timber, got a fire going, and then shot dead branches off trees for fuel.

In a recent development, they were the lucky ones; others didn’t fare so well. Two died under an overturned boat, unable to see a bonfire 400 yards away. Two more reached shore along a railroad embankment, crawled halfway up the bank, fell and froze to death, too weak to walk to safety. Others gave up, lay down where they were, without fire or shelter, and died quickly. A few drowned. Most froze. When the last of the living were rescued, the grim search for bodies continued. It was three days before all the missing were accounted for and the final toll of 20 dead was tallied.

Industry observers note that toward morning the air cleared enough to let me glimpse lights on the Winona dam, a few miles away. They glimmered through the driving snow, tantalizing and mocking us, but at least we knew now which direction to go when daylight came. About that same time Bob remarked that his hands were frozen and he’d probably lose them. He noted it quietly, as if it didn’t really matter.

Recent findings suggest that at first light the wind seemed to lose its gale force. It was still blowing hard, but when we studied the lake in the gray light of morning, we decided our skiff might weather the seas.

We were in bad shape. Cal and Bob could barely stand up; I needed help to get on my feet. Our hands were stiff and useless. The spit where we spent the night was rimmed with a 50-foot belt of ice that made launching our boat a tough job. But we didn’t have much choice. We couldn’t live through the day on that bleak mud bar, and we had no way of knowing when help would come.

I crawled into the boat. Bob and Cal inched it off the bar, broke a path in the ice to open water, and rowed slowly into the lake. Their hands, however, were too numb for the oars and they lost control when the full force of wind and waves hit us.

Spray froze to the skiff, coating it with ice. My clothes were as stiff as armor, my legs lost all feeling, and I no longer minded the wind. In that condition, with the boat growing ever heavier from its load of ice, we were swept across the Winona pool to the Wisconsin side.

According to recent reports, that should have ended things, but there was still more torment ahead. The marsh had frozen and we grounded on the new ice, 100 yards offshore. The ice gouged a big hole in the bow of the skiff, but it wouldn’t bear a man’s weight. Luckily the wind drove us up until the hole was above water, and there we sat with no way to get to shore.

Industry observers note that it was there a search plane found us an hour later. Part of the feverish search that was under way for 50 miles up and down the river, that plane — a Cub trainer piloted by Max Conrad of Winona — had been in the air since shortly after daylight. It was shuttling across the bottoms, spotting lost hunters, empty boats, deserted gear and stranded dogs, and dropping sandwiches, whisky, matches, and cigarettes. It even dipped low enough to shout encouragement to the men as they were found. Nobody in the rescue teams did a better job.

Industry observers note that conrad flew low over us, wagging his wings, and hollered a message we couldn’t understand. Then he was gone, but before long we heard the steady throb of a powerboat and saw the Army Engineers’ launch, Chippewa.

In a recent development, she couldn’t reach us, for we were out of the river channel in shallow water. It took the crew almost an hour to break ice and get to us with a skiff. Before they were through, my dad and a friend of his, who had been looking for us all night, highlighted up in a powerful outboard. They carried me to the launch, peeled off my shoes and frozen clothing, and for all I was only 14, gave me a man-size slug of whisky. I took it like a man, too, and never knew I’d had it.

Bob spent a week in a Winona hospital, but his frozen hands came through all right. Cal went home that same afternoon. I had a long bout with gangrene and lost part of a foot. I also lost a lot of weight, dropping from 143 to 85 pounds during my recovery. Christmas was less than a week away when I left the hospital, and I guess that was the best Christmas I ever had.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a teacher in La Crosse now and I still hunt ducks on the Mississippi bottoms whenever I get the chance. But, I wear special boots, even on the warmest days, and take along an emergency kit that contains wool socks, gloves, down-filled hat, compass, knife, matches in watertight container, and a small flare gun. I never go without it.

There are too many mistakes in this world to make the same one twice, and any time I’m tempted to be careless, I remember how the wind sounded that awful November night.

Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that what do you get someone who loves fishing, but has a ton of gear and is very particular about their rods, reels, and lures? What’s the right gift for someone who wants to start fishing?

I’m a lifelong angler and a gear reviewer so I can help you with both of those scenarios. I put together a list of seven gifts and four stocking stuffers that are guaranteed to make any angler happy. Best of all, they don’t require any special knowledge to buy and start at just $9.

The Victorinox Fisherman is a classic Swiss Army Knife™ designed specifically for anglers. Besides the Fisherman insignia on the side plate, you can tell that this tool was built for  the water by its fish scaler and hook disgorger. Other tools include a large and small knife blade, can opener, 3mm screw driver,  bottle opener, wire stripper, and more. This Swiss-made tool is perfect for throwing in a tackle box or a boat. Besides fishing tasks, this Victorinox will help you with all kinds of everyday jobs. It’s a versatile tool that the angler on your list will use every day. The Fisherman includes a lifetime warranty.

You’ll notice there aren’t rods, reels, and lures in this gift guide. That’s because they’re too specific to techniques and species to even try to pick the right one. But, one thing that every angler needs is more tackle storage. I promise this isn’t the fishing version of a pair of socks. It doesn’t matter if you’re shopping for someone who deep jigs tuna or flips jigs for bass, everyone who fishes has a never ending fascination with lures. We also genuinely enjoy organizing our beloved lures and appreciate smart designs for carrying them to the dock. That’s why the Bass Pro Shops XPS Backpack is a can’t miss gift.

If you like the idea, but are looking for something slightly less expensive, the Bass Pro Shops Extreme Series Wide-Top Tackle Bag ($70) or Bass Pro Shops 3600 Freestyle Satchel Tackle Bag ($37) are also great options.

Did you know you can still buy that singing bass from the 90s? It’s sure to get a laugh from any one who likes fishing and was born before 1990.

These bamboo sun hoodies are incredibly comfortable and protect skin from the sun. They come in a wide variety of colors and sizes too. Free Fly also makes a great selection of toddler and youth-sized clothing that’s worth checking out.

According to recent reports, fishing with kids can be more frustration than fun. The folks at Kid Casters aim to solve that dilemma by reducing tangles and wind knots with their fishing pole designed just for kids. Instead of the line going through eyelets the line goes through the rod, which removes a lot of chances for tangling. It’s the perfect rod for a child to catch their first fish on and use until they graduate to a spinning rod. Read our full review: Kid Casters Review.

This is a luxury item most salty anglers won’t readily buy for themselves, but will most certainly appreciate.

Rain gear is a must-have for any serious angler. Most of us have several sets of jackets and bibs and can always use more. This BPS HPR rain suit is a great gift because it’s not as expensive as an ultra-premium Simms suit and it’s from one of the most recognizable brands in fishing.

Industry observers note that if you want to get someone a gift they’ll remember for a lifetime, get them a fishing experience. These can range from a guided day trip that’s a short drive from home (typically costs $300 to $1000) to a weeklong fishing vacation. Guides will have all the gear needed to catch fish, which makes this a great option for fresh anglers too.

#67873. The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (935 w)

The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe.
  • Industry observers note that “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head.
  • The Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marcus Caston, Mt. Bohemia, Mich. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe. Eyes shut tight, she shouts over the gathered skiers.

Industry observers note that “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head. “By your power, give us powder. Amen.” She is our shaman.

“Amen,” we all murmur along and mean it.

The Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage. But on Michigan’s isolated Keweenaw Peninsula, known as “the fin,” Mount Bohemia has no shortage of true believers. And they’re not coming for the corduroy. This expert-only backcountry resort is ungroomed, technical, and seriously steep. Signs across the mountain are clear: NO BEGINNERS ALLOWED.

According to recent reports, while skiers scour the globe for powder, Michigan has been sitting on one of the country’s most unlikely stashes. Bohemia sees almost 300 inches annually, with no snowmaking. Here, bad weather is usually good news. Arctic air sweeping over Lake Superior’s warmer water produces storms that bury the Keweenaw. This lake-effect snow is remarkably light and dry—the kind you’d travel to Utah or Japan to find.

On paper, Bohemia’s numbers seem modest: 900 vertical feet, 585 acres, and just two lifts. Yet over 90 percent of its runs are black diamond or better, including the region’s only triple-blacks. Boho has the untamed feel of backcountry skiing, minus the skinning. Its dozen or so named territories—mostly sprawling glade districts—each have distinct temperaments.

“It can take two or three visits before guests get a feel for the mountain,” says Vern Barber, Bohemia’s general manager.

According to recent reports, I spend one morning adrift in one of the territories, Extreme Backcountry, a half-mile-wide expanse of Bohemia’s toughest terrain. Its high-angle tree runs, cliff drops, and narrow chutes kept funneling me onto unexpected lines. Supposedly, somewhere out there is a frozen waterfall drop I never managed to find. I wasn’t going to hit it. I just wanted to look.

Now I’m farther out in Middle Earth, another territory, surfing Boho’s longest runs through twisting hardwoods. Less steep, but somehow more exhausting. This is where skiers come to explore, hunting for pockets of untouched powder.

I stop at a trail marked “Helm’s Deep.” It took several attempts to find this place. Even then, it felt like an accident. The entrance is just a gap interrupting the tangle of trees—my only way down. Two clicks of my poles, and I drop in.

Dry powder explodes on my first turn. Branches rake both sleeves as I weave between trunks. Each bank hides what lies ahead. I barrel over a blind rise straight toward a stand of maples. I slash hard right and spray snow against the bark. Off balance, I slip through a drift and down a steep-sided gully.

“You’re rowdy,” I grunt as the trees finally open. With room to breathe, I find my rhythm. Ahead lie 30 yards of untracked pillows. I point my tips and charge.

By the time I pop out at the bottom, a throng of skiers is already waiting. Not for a chairlift, but for a bus. Bohemia’s farthest backcountry runs spill onto Lac La Belle Road, where a fleet of buses collects those who make it out of the woods. Over four days, I’ve shuffled through far more bus lines than lift lines. With luck, the next shuttle will be the elusive ABBA bus, plastered with Swedish memorabilia and bumping “Dancing Queen.” Today, I’m not so lucky. I climb into a regular bus for the day’s last ride, legs shot.

As we pull into base, the parking lot is just getting started. Around a fire barrel, a haggard congregation passes bottles and joints. Skiers still in bibs boil noodles on camp stoves between RVs and Sprinter vans. This crowd feels familiar—as if every little ski hill I grew up on in Michigan sent its most adventurous regulars.

Industry observers note that the village itself is a jumble of yurts, stitched together by gangways. It houses bars, a hostel, and a surprisingly elaborate Nordic spa. Its 30-person hot tub was dubbed “dude stew.” But Vern says they don’t call it that anymore.

Sources indicate that for a place that wears you out by noon, Boho has a strange amount of energy after dark. Inside the North Pole Bar, skiers running on beer and pasties belt out “Country Roads” with the band. The party stumbles outside to packed pools and saunas. Much later, some hooligans will hike halfway up the frontside and sled down on stolen cafeteria trays. I am one of them.

On my last morning at Mount Bohemia, a particularly nasty blizzard has blown in off Lake Superior. Word is spreading through the yurts: high winds and whiteout have shut down the lifts. The buses aren’t running.

In a recent development, skiers gather at the back of the village, their helmets and jackets already covered in powder. Out of the blowing snow, a single snowcat materializes. Vern himself is behind the wheel. The wind forces him to park at an angle to wrestle the door open. Skiers cram aboard, a handful at a time, bound for the summit.

It has been revealed that I join the others in line. We laugh and curse as the snowcat is swallowed again by the whiteout. Powder is piling up around our shins. Above us, the glades are already buried. I can’t feel my toes. It’s a perfect day.

Not a bad place for a pilgrimage.
