For the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot. For hunters on a budget, the SpyPoint Flex-M2 is the pick. Need maximum detection range, choose the Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0. For the sharpest images, the Stealth Cam Deceptor Max 3.0 leads the field.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s. I remember walking laps around the local Walmart, waiting for the one-hour photo lab to process my prints. Most of the time, it was 24 images of a branch that the wind blew back and forth. Occasionally, I’d get a deer—sometimes even a good buck.

According to recent reports, trail cams have come a long way since, and, of course, cellular trail cameras dominate the scene today. If you want to learn all you can about the critters you hunt without setting foot in the woods other than to change batteries or move a camera or two, cellular trail cameras are the way to go. But which cell cams?

To help you figure out which models are right for you, I spent two months running and testing the latest newly introduced-for-2026 cell cams in my backyard and on a nearby 700-acre whitetail property in Colorado. Testing conditions were difficult. Every camera was exposed to heavy wind, a 60-day average high temperature of 95.7 degrees, rain, and hail that damaged roofs. The good news: There were no flops. I would have no reservations running any of the new cellular cams below anywhere in the country. That remarked, some proved better than others depending on what your value most. So, let’s dive in. Here are the best cellular trail cameras of 2026.

One complaint I’ve always had about cellular trail cameras is the antennas, as they are always breaking off in backpacks or the back seat of my truck. Mother Nature has her way with them, dropping dead branches and crushing skinny, side-mounted antennas. I’ve even broken a couple by catching the antenna in my pant leg while walking to a stand in the dark.

Sources indicate that browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV features an innovative, wide, blade-style antenna located in the center of the trail camera. It’s extra-sturdy and folds back and locks into the back of the main camera housing for easy, secure transport. The high-gain antenna also grabbed the most available network more quickly than any other camera in this year’s test.

Sources indicate that the MAX HD DV uses the same straightforward interface on the camera’s lower housing behind the lock-and-latch door that Browning customers are used to and appreciate. The 1.5-inch LED screen is bright, and the soft-push buttons don’t stick. When you turn the camera on, the LED screen displays a 10-second countdown before you close the door.

You have plenty of options when setting up the camera via the Strike Fore Wireless app. I recommend running the camera on Medium photo quality with High video. Avoid the Ultra-quality setting for both photo and video to save battery life, as the quality is plenty good without it. All images are delivered in HD, so there are no grainy thumbnails or waiting for the camera to trigger again to view a high-resolution photo. Videos with audio are ultra-clean. The camera took very few false triggers, and I love the user-adjustable flash.

Over 60 days in the field, Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV captured deer, day and night, in the center of the frame from 10 feet to 120 feet. Browning lists a detection range of 100 feet, but this camera exceeds that distance.

It has been revealed that using just 8 standard alkaline batteries, camera life was excellent, holding at around 90 percent after 60 days afield. At night, the MAX HD DV uses Illuma-Smart technology to adjust the flash for crisp, clear nighttime images, and its detection range remains over 100 feet after dark. This trail camera was built to handle extreme weather and keep delivering images.

Industry observers note that the only area Browning Trail Cameras needs to improve upon is its Strike Force Wireless app. The app functions well but struggles to categorize photos in the main image Library when you’re running more than one camera.

Other than that, Browning’s newly introduced MAX HD DV is everything I want in a cellular trail camera. It captures HD photos and 1080p video with audio, doesn’t spook deer, and has given me zero hassles after 60 days afield. It’s a tad pricey, but you’ll more than make up for it in batteries.

Industry observers note that moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar is the best solar-powered cellular trail camera I’ve ever used, and, at $169.99—including the solar panel—it is priced right. The panel itself is simple and effective; it slides and locks into the top of the camera, and you can angle the it to ensure it gathers as much sunlight as possible throughout the day.

I’ve had two Edge 4 Solar cameras in the field longer than any other cellular trail camera in this year’s test. They were the first cameras delivered to my doorstep, and when I get a newly introduced product, I like to start using it right away. Using Moultrie’s $50 (aftermarket) Power Mag II battery pack in tandem with the solar panel, my battery life has never dipped below 80 percent. This means you can stay out of the woods and reduce your human footprint, which is the main goal of cellular trail cameras.

Recent findings suggest that setup is super easy. Like all the trail cameras in this year’s test, the Edge 4 Solar connects to the strongest available cellular network. I like the new internal interface. The white push up/down, on/off button is gone. Moultrie added a twist-and-turn dial that doesn’t stick. The battery life indicator is back, and once powered on, all three lights (Not Connected-red, Connecting-yellow, Connected-green) turn solid. Then, the Connecting light flashes slowly, and after about one minute, the green Connected light turns solid green. At this point, the camera is fully operational. It pairs seamlessly with Moultrie’s app and is one of the most user-friendly cellular trail cameras in this year’s test.

Aside from the newly introduced interface, Moultrie made other changes that earned the new Edge 4 Solar our top honor. The most notable is better nighttime image quality and a reduction in false triggers. Moultrie’s new Night Clarity feature uses enhanced low-glow IR LEDs to help illuminate the backdrop and boost edge-to-edge sharpness. Nighttime images are excellent, and every image, day or night, is delivered in HD.

Last year, especially toward the end of my 60-day testing period, my Edge 3 started triggering when nothing was there. The Edge 4 Pro Solar has not followed suit.

Recent findings suggest that another new and purposeful feature is Buck Shot. Moultrie AI technology detects mature bucks and sends a zoomed-in, max-resolution image. I really enjoyed this feature. Typically, action on my lease doesn’t heat up until mid-October, as few bucks summer on the property. However, this year has been different. A pair of shooter bucks—bucks I passed last fall—are semi-regular on an oat field. The Edge 4 Solar sends me a zoomed-in picture every single time either buck trips the camera.

In a partnership with onX, Edge 4 cameras are instantly pinned the second they are placed. By the end of September, I will have multiple trail cameras—cellular and conventional—spread across the West and Midwest. Too often, I get in a hurry and forget to drop a camera pin when I’m using trail cameras. However, if I’m using Moultrie, I can forget, and the map-pinning technology saves me.

Other standout features of the Edge 4 Solar include a tough-as-nails housing with an IP67 waterproof rating. Both of my Edge 4 Solar cameras have been exposed to torrential downpours and hail. Not a drop of moisture has gotten inside, and after months in the field, the cameras and the panels look like they just came out of the box.

Sources indicate that at under $80, SpyPoint’s Flex-M2 is a solid cellular trail camera. It comes with a two-year warranty, and SpyPoint offers a pair of M2s for just $129.99, which is an excellent deal.

Industry observers note that my first experience with the Flex-M2 was in Montana while helping a buddy set up his whitetail property. The Flex-M2 is compact, lightweight, easy to set up, and connects to the strongest cellular network in the area. Its .4-second advertised trigger speed proved accurate and reliable in my testing, and the camera captured deer at distances beyond 90 feet.

When I returned from Montana, I added a pair of Flex-M2 cameras to my Colorado property. Both have been on the property for 60 days and send crisp images and 1080p video with solid audio to my phone daily. They have withstood torrid summer heat, rain and hail, and continue to impress me.

Industry observers note that one issue I’ve had with both cameras is battery life. Using standard AA alkaline batteries, both Flex-M2 models drained relatively quickly. That stated, when I swapped the battery trays for SpyPoint’s LIT-22 rechargeable power packs, battery life improved significantly. Set to Photo-only mode with medium photo resolution and a multi-shot setting of two images per trigger, my battery life has been holding steady above 80 percent.

Setup and connection time was straightforward and quick. I like the positive bottom latch lock, and the raised, gridded on/off switch is easy to operate. Once clicked on, the cellular lights blink until the camera receives a signal. Next, the status light turns blue. Once connected, the blue LED extinguishes, and the green LED on the outside of the camera blinks for 10 seconds. Once the green light stops flashing, the camera is in transmission mode.

Sources indicate that the Flex-M2 was the smallest cellular trail cam in this year’s test, and the long antenna is detachable for easy transport. Once you place your M2 in the field, it immediately shows up on the SpyPoint app map feature.

It has been revealed that the camera occasionally produces false triggers, but I was able to reduce this by setting the sensitivity to Medium, and the camera still picks up deer-sized game beyond 90 feet. The BuckTracker feature has done its job. Buck pics are slugged correctly, and I’ve yet to have the technology slug a doe as a buck. BuckTracker even correctly identified and a 3-inch spick at 64 feet.

In the end, Spypoint’s Flex-M2 gets our 2026 Best Value award because while it might not have all the bells and whistles of other cell scouters, it does the job—and does it for about half the price of several others.

Last year, Tactacam’s Reveal Ultra took home top honors in our cellular trail camera test. Its predecessor, the Reveal Pro 4.0, nearly earned the cell-cam maker a repeat performance, but fell just a tad short. It is, however, a cell scouter that every hunter should take a close look at.

Recent findings suggest that like the Ultra, the Pro 4.0 features Low-Glow and No-Glow flash settings. I love this option. Low-Glow works great for fields, logging roads, or any camera location where detection range needs a bump. No-Glow is ideal for tight timber trail crossings, river crossings, scrapes, or any area where detection range matters less and stealth matters more. The Reveal Pro 4.0 doesn’t spook deer. When set in No-Glow, deer don’t even glance at the camera, and new Dual Image Sensors improve day and nighttime photos.

Sources indicate that another stealth boost is that the slight click that previous Reveal models produced when capturing a nighttime image is gone. According to Reveal, the Dual Sensors—one stacked on top of the other—produce cleaner nighttime images without the audible click associated with a low-light filter. Once you set the Reveal Pro 4.0 in the woods, it’s a ghost, which is just what you want.

Battery life on last year’s Ultra model was solid and given that the Reveal app lets consumers select camera sensitivity levels between 0 and 9, false triggers have always been few and far between. However, Reveal wanted the Pro 4.0 to have a longer run time, especially when battery-draining features such as larger image sizes, longer video durations, and Live View Mode are used.

According to recent reports, the battery-life boosting answer is Reveal’s FlexPack R5 and R10 Power Systems. The upcoming interface location on the camera’s right side, in the upper-right corner, lets the bottom of the camera (the battery box) pull away. The design was well thought out and is an overlooked feature of the new Pro 4.0. With the battery box removed, aftermarket R5 (5,000 mAh) and R10 (10,000 mAh) Power Systems plug in much like rechargeable batteries found on power tools.

I ran the camera for 15 days using standard Alkaline AA batteries and for 15 days using the FlexPack R5. There is no question the Power Systems increase battery life and are worth the money. During its 15-day run time, the 4.0 with R5 triggered 332 times. I requested 28 videos and purposely activated Live View 10 times to further test battery life. At the end of the test, the camera still had 95 percent battery life remaining.

According to recent reports, one small blip with this camera is that of all the cellular models I tested, the Pro 4.0 had the slowest connection time. I ran a pair of Pro 4.0s, and the average time from powering on the cameras to receiving my first test photo in an area with 4 bars of AT&T 5G LTE service was 12 minutes. I’m not sure what that was about, but both cameras struggled to get a signal and start transmitting images. Once the camera were fully connected, though, trigger speed was excellent, detection range was spot-on, and images and videos were clear and colorful.

If it weren’t for the SpyPoint’s crazy-low price, Stealth Cam’s Deceptor Max 3.0 would have won our Best Photo Quality and Best Value awards. At just under $120, this cellular trail camera should be on every hunter’s radar. Past Stealth Cam cellular models I’ve test produced too many false triggers and had relatively poor battery life. Not so with this one. After 60 days in the field, the Deceptor Max 3.0 has sent only three images to my phone that didn’t show a deer, thanks to the camera’s new False Trigger Filter feature, and after 723 photos and 23 20-second videos, the battery is at 90 percent.

According to recent reports, with its No Glow flash, the Max 3.0 has not spooked deer, near or far. Trigger speed is excellent, and with the Command app and the camera set to Standard blur reduction, images have been crisp and clean. The camera captured a doe blazing past at 1:30 a.m. in the center of the frame. The doe was in focus, and 15 seconds later, so were a pair of coyotes hot on her trail.

The Deceptor Max 3.0 lets people set photo quality to 50MP. That makes for really good pics, but it’s more than most folks need and eats up battery life. I tested the camera at 4MP and 8MP, and the Max 3.0 produced the clearest, brightest, and most colorful images in this year’s test.

According to recent reports, A cool feature that Stealth Cam added is Rack Alert, which sends a message to your smartphone letting you know the exact moment a racked deer steps in front of your Max 3.0. This feature worked great on my Colorado lease, and my Oklahoma buddy purchased three Max 3.0 cameras and set them over feeders. He told me he never looks at his image library until Rack Alert informs him. He trusts the technology, and so do I.

Upgraded antenna pulls poor cell service.

The solar cord is big, long, and clunky.

It has been revealed that the Interceptor is not new for this year, but it one of our favorites from last year’s test, winning our Best Trigger Speed award. Covert upped its game 2025, producing a new solar cell cam scouter that’s lightning fast and offers tons of great features. The Interceptor Solar was easy to set up. Downloading the Covert app, building an account, and getting the cam operational took less than five minutes.

The camera’s paddle-style antenna proved rigid and robust, even in heavy winds. Covert lists the trigger speed at .4 seconds, but my testing showed an average of .24 seconds. That data was obtained using two different stopwatches, as well as a chip time card that runners use.

Recent findings suggest that when charged to full, the camera’s on-board solar keeps the unit running, even in dense timber. Several times, the Interceptor got down to less than 30 percent battery life at night, but it would still center images in the frame, and deliver good-qualiy photos and real-time 2K video. During the day, even without direct sun exposure, battery life would rise to 80 percent. When set on a pond and alfalfa plot, the battery never dipped below 60 percent and would achieve a full charge during the day.

It has been revealed that covert lists the effective flash range at 90 feet, and my testing confirmed this. I appreciate the 2-inch screen, though very little of the actual setup work is accomplished using the camera. Everything is done in the Covert app. The Covert Interceptor Solar features on-board GPS, so you can’t lose your camera, uses 8 AA batteries as backup, and comes with a 2-year warranty.

It has been revealed that my only complaint on this otherwise excellent camera is the long and bulky cord that connects the on-board solar unit to the camera. Be sure to take some Gorilla tape or some zip-ties to roll the cord up and tuck it out of the way. But that’s the end of my quibbling. The camera took only 11 false images during its 20-day testing period and captured a full-sprint coyote in the center of the frame, with no blur. The camera does have species recognition, which works well, but it is a service that costs extra, and I would deactivate it. Like most hunters, I know what a doe and buck deer look like.

Requires a minimum of two cameras.

Longer setup and deployment time.

Recent findings suggest that cuddeback continues to offer it’s CuddeLink system. The nice thing about Cuddelink is that once you have the Home camera and a cellular proposal, you can run as many as 24 cameras on that same plan, which sarts as low as $10 per month. I opted for the $40 plan to receive unlimited photos. I tested the CuddeLink L-Series Cell Home unit ($130) and CuddeLink L-Seires cell cam ($150), so my initial investment was more. Still, I could add additional CuddeLink-compatible cell cameras (up to 24) to my $40 per month plan.

Recent findings suggest that operationally, the Home (CuddeLink) and Remote (L-Series) systems are sound. However, you’ll need to read heavy instruction manuals to get them linked to the same chain and go through the settings. It’s not a problem, and it’s not difficult. However, it will take you some time to learn the ins and outs of the system. This duo took much longer to learn about and get in the field than other cameras. That mentioned, one the initial system is setup, it’s easy to add more cams and daisy chain them into the system.

The CuddeLink L-Series comes in multiple models. I tested the Zoom IR. The photo quality is only decent, but what I do like about the camera is that it uses a center-angle Fresnel lens that increases detection range and zooms the photo in. I’m not in love with having the Home camera and then linking cameras to it, especially cellular, but the system does work and does have the potential to save you money.

Internal screen viewer to aid setup.

Among the most simple setups in the test.

Night pics suffer a bit at longer ranges.

This camera is not new by any means, but don’t let that stop you. High-quality photos, a lightning-fast trigger, and easy setup are a significant pluses with the CelluCore Live. The impressive 0.2-second trigger speed helps capture sharp images and can keep up with fast-moving deer. Plus, the fast image recovery time and subtle infrared flash elevate this cam to the next level. The only thing keeping this camera from the top models is a moderate detection range, and the data plans are, well, not much. It’s not cheap either, though you may be able to find deals.

Thanks to some fantastic friends, I have access to over 700 acres of prime Colorado whitetail dirt, which has proven to be the perfect testing ground for our annual cellular trail camera test. There are plenty of deer to get pictures of and a combination of summer heat, thunderstorms, wind, and extreme temperature fluctuations tests the cameras’ durability.

Since I conducted last year’s cellular trail camera test, I had all the apps on my smartphone. All I did was add cameras, adjust sensitivity levels, check connectivity, and dial in the settings. For testing, I set all cameras to photo resolutions between 4 and 8MP, 1080p video, and two images per trigger.

According to recent reports, before field deployment, I tested all the cams in my backyard. I wanted to make sure they paired with their corresponding app and that photos were transmitting. I set cones at measured distances and walked, jogged, and sprinted past each camera at 10-foot intervals, from 20 to 120 feet. I repeated this process in the field as well. I tested trigger speed and detection zines during daylight and nighttime hours.

In the field, I rotated all the cameras between four areas: a three-way trail intersection, the lower end of an alfalfa plot, a pond, and a community scrape deer use year-round. Throughout the test—over the course of 60 days—I evaluated each camera’s durability, ease of setup, price, battery life, image and video quality, detection range, and trigger speed. Finally, when all the testing and evaluating is done, I picked our winners.

According to recent reports, ease of setup and quick connection to the camera’s corresponding app save time and frustration. Not every hunter is a tech wizard, and thanks to the simplicity of this year’s camera crop, you don’t have to be. The only camera I had to fight with in terms of connectivity and transmission was the Reveal Pro 4.0. However, that fight was minor.

According to recent reports, many cell-cam makers are skipping grainy thumbnails and going straight to all-HD all the time. I like this. Cell cams have made me very impatient. When I get a picture of a buck, I don’t want to download a grainy image to my computer and then study it for hours trying to determine whether the buck is a shooter while I wait for a high-resolution image to come through. Cams that automatically send hi-res pics get bonus points in my book. Choose a cellular trail camera that lets you adjust image and video quality and set both high enough to avoid compromising image quality but not so high that battery life suffers.

Trigger speed matters, especially during the rut. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have rapid trigger speed, quicker recovery times, and some type of anti-blur technology. Summertime deer don’t often test a camera’s trigger speed, but during the rut, when a doe comes running past, you want that doe centered in the frame, and the camera needs to recover fast enough that the big buck hot on her heels gets his picture taken too. The cellular trail cameras I tested this year have fast triggers and quick recovery times.

It has been revealed that I prefer cellular trail cameras with an adjustable flash. Some come with adjustable flash settings, while others adjust the flash setting automatically based on the time of day. Stay away from high-glow LEDs and any cell camera that produces a flash that spooks deer. All the cameras I tested this year didn’t bother deer a bit.

Cellular trail-cam manufacturers embellish a lot of things. One thing they don’t embellish—or at least didn’t embellish this year, is detection range. If anything, they underplayed it. Detection range is the maximum distance at which a camera will detect an object. Typically, the farther an object is from the camera, the larger it needs to be to be detected by the camera. Anything at over 100 feet is impressive.

I like a very basic and straightforward app that allows me immediate access to the camera’s settings. I like to try all the technologies and features of every cell camera I test. The better the app, the easier it is to swap between settings, organize photos, etc. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have fancy features. Take advantage of them and see if you find them beneficial. Some of them drain battery life; others don’t. Find out what works best for you and the area you hunt.

In a recent development, the development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear. As much as we enjoy spending time in nature during the winter months, we hate cold hands. It’s hard to concentrate on your hunt or effectively work if your fingers are so cold you can no longer feel them. For anyone with arthritis or other hand pain, it can be downright painful to venture out in winter. Luckily, battery-operated heating elements are here to change the game.

Wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore. That’s why we’ve done the homework for you. It doesn’t matter if you need something for work or for ice fishing, we’ve got you covered with the best heated gloves available for cold weather.

When it comes to battery life, the Ororo heated gloves—which feature three heat settings—performed better than I expected. I was able to run the gloves on the maximum temperature setting for approximately three to four hours and on the medium setting for at least five. However, the low setting was where they really shined. These gloves ran for a solid eight hours on that setting. Because they were so warm even without turning on the electricity, I highly doubt I’ll ever use the medium and high settings.

My only real complaint is that I feel the dexterity could be better. The insulation makes the fingers a bit too fat for shooting a rifle or shotgun. But the grip on the palms and fingers has a tacky feel to it that’s perfectly suited for working with shovels or other hand tools where super fine control isn’t needed. I’ll be using these to clear the driveway of snow once winter returns to Michigan. These gloves would also be excellent for operating a tractor, ATV, or snowmobile in cold temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that the Savior gloves are plenty warm without an electric feature. But they also feature larger 2200 mAh batteries that help keep your fingers toasty through longer days outdoors. Because they are waterproof and thick, you can wear these gloves whenever there is snow or slush on the ground. The windproof quality makes them an excellent choice for work or riding a motorcycle, too. They are thick, so there is some dexterity loss. But Savior Heat made the button for heat control quite large, so you can easily operate it without removing the gloves.

In a recent development, these gloves are a hair on the expensive side. But that’s to be expected for this battery size and durability. While we like these gloves best for work—like construction or ranch work—they are versatile enough to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios.

Industry observers note that surprisingly, there are not a lot of dedicated hunting gloves featuring electronic heating. This pair is both windproof and waterproof—perfect for hunters who don’t like to head in once the weather takes a turn for the worst. The 7.4V battery packs will help the warming functions last through a full day in frigid temperatures, and the buttons are large enough that you can operate them while wearing the gloves. Plus, they have fingertips that can operate a touchscreen.

According to recent reports, the three heat settings allow you to customize just how warm your hands are (and the soft cotton material is extra cozy). However, we wish there were more camo patterns other than Realtree Edge. Not that the deer will notice or care, but some of us like our camo outfits to match.

The Snow Deer gloves offer surprising dexterity for thicker gloves. They are suitable for everything from hunting to motorcycling thanks to the sheep leather palms that help provide additional grip. The heated wires in this pair of gloves extends completely to each of the fingers, making them a great option for anyone with arthritis or circulation issues in the hands. There is also fleece in the glove liners to help retain heat and repel moisture.

These gloves have a shorter battery life than some of the other options on this list. But they’re very well constructed. Features like the sheepskin palm and fleece lining add a lot of additional value for the money here. If you need gloves that are versatile for more than one outdoor activity, these are the ones to consider.

Recent findings suggest that these featherweight gloves offer a great deal of dexterity that’s ideal for work or recreational activities in bitter cold conditions. The extra reinforcement of the palm and inside of the fingers further emphasizes the fact that these gloves are made with cold weather activities in mind. You can also cinch the cuff tight to prevent extra snow and wind from getting in at the wrists and dropping your core body temperature.

Sources indicate that these heated gloves have a slightly shorter run time than we’d expect for a battery of this size. It runs for about two hours on high, three hours on medium, and five hours on low. Extra batteries are a necessity if you need them super toasty for long periods. That noted, we think the shortened runtime is a decent tradeoff for the extra dexterity offered by these gloves.

In a recent development, for the gloves I tested, I first made sure the batteries were fully charged. I then ran each pair on the highest warmth settings to assess the battery life of each glove. I also wore the gloves while performing a variety of activities both recreational and for work. This allowed me to evaluate the comfort and dexterity of each pair. Additionally, I considered the following factors when making my decisions:.

In a recent development, there are a few different types of heated gloves. The most popular style utilizes an electronic battery system and heated wires in the fabric, which is extremely effective for staying warm. The downside is that gloves like this are often expensive and require frequent recharging. Most have a battery life of six to eight hours depending on the set intensity level.

There are also gloves and mittens with small pockets for chemical hand warmers. One pro to this style is the reduced cost. Of course, you can only use the disposable hand warmers once before tossing them in the trash. There’s also waste from the airtight wrappers this style of warmer is sealed inside, so it’s not exactly the greenest solution out there. But you don’t have to worry about charging any batteries and you can quickly replace the warmers in the field once they lose heat.

Recent findings suggest that when picking a glove, think about how you proposal to use it. Thicker gloves are great if all you plan to do is ride a snowmobile or ATV. However, they can rapidly become useless if you need to do more delicate tasks. Thick gloves can make it difficult to squeeze the trigger on a rifle or work on an engine. Think about dexterity and how much you’ll need. At the same time, be careful not to buy gloves that are too small or too tight.

Industry observers note that for gloves that will be used primarily for working, it pays to go with thicker materials like leather that are built to take abuse. Ideally, the palms will be reinforced for heavier tasks like ranch work. It’s not a bad idea to go for work gloves that are waterproof—or at least water-resistant—either.

It has been revealed that many clothing manufacturers are now making their gloves with at least one specialized fingertip designed for operating a screen. The quality of these fingertips varies depending on the glove. Some gloves just don’t have the dexterity for typing or sending emails effectively. But quality ones make for great hunting gloves when you want to stay in touch with your buddies without losing any warmth.

Mittens are almost always warmer than gloves, and that includes heated mittens. This is simply because mittens allow your fingers to share warmth and slow heat loss. Of course, this comes at the cost of dexterity for more precise tasks.

It can be a bit of a balancing act to find the right fit for warm gloves. Go with gloves that are too loose and you lose dexterity and warmth. If the gloves are too tight, they might cut off circulation. The ideal solution is to find gloves that fall somewhere in between. The gloves shouldn’t be so tight they feel restricting, but they also shouldn’t fall off your hands.

According to recent reports, waterproof capabilities vary from glove to glove. Some have that feature built in standard while others may need to be kept out of the snow and ice to function properly. Be sure to read the fine print on any pair you buy first. Most work gloves are built rather ruggedly and will handle a little water.

While the technology for heated gloves continues to improve, the Ororo gloves were a standout for us in terms of battery life. These large versatile gloves will get you through the worst sub-zero temperatures that nature can dish out, and the competitive price makes them a solid option for gearing up for another long winter. Even if you choose another pair on this list, the best heated gloves will keep your digits nice and warm all season long.

Is Early-Season Skiing Worth It? Here’s the Case for Going.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture.
  • The solution is early-season skiing.
  • Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Vail Resorts).

According to recent reports, there’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture. But too often, the things that make skiing great get overshadowed by cost and crowds. It’s hard to find your flow when the run is crowded, and even the best ski day is hard to enjoy when lodging, lift tickets, and lunch leave you financially stretched.

The solution is early-season skiing. Few people book a ski trip in November or early December, and even local skiers tend to be unenthused. But I think they’re missing out. In fact, early season is one of my favorite times to ski. Early season turns have led to breakthroughs in my technique, and it’s one of the only times when the mountain feels small enough to meet up with friends.

Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.

And the things that make skiing less appealing are non-concerns.

The cost of an early ski season trip can be half or even a third of what you’ll pay just a few weeks later. In Jackson Hole, for example, if you visit in early December, rather than Christmas week, you’ll pay $85 for a lift ticket instead of $340. Similarly, a room at the ultra-luxe slopeside Hotel Terra Jackson Hole increases by $600 a night based on whether you stay in early or late December. The same goes for big ski weeks like spring break and Presidents’ Day—and the weeks in between aren’t much cheaper.

And then there’s the fact that when you’re not skiing at the same time as everyone else, every aspect of the day (or your entire trip) becomes more enjoyable. You’ll get in more skiing thanks to shorter (or nonexistent) lift lines, and you don’t have to worry about running into someone on the way down. And when you aren’t one of 10 people waiting in line for rental gear or a table at the restaurant, you’ll get warmer, more personalized service. (Plus, in early season, everyone is fresh and excited for the season ahead, not tired and over it.).

In a recent development, when the mountain is fully open, and everyone’s ski legs are firing, the pressure to go massive is real. It can be difficult and dangerous to try to keep up, especially if you’re upcoming to skiing or it’s your first (or only) ski trip of the year.

According to recent reports, but in the early season, everyone is still getting their ski legs under them, and the skiing is more about fine-tuning your technique and rebuilding muscle. There’s nothing showy about it, and most people leave their egos at home.

According to recent reports, the biggest argument against early season skiing is the lack of snow. Indeed, in the early season, the snow hasn’t had time to accumulate. Often, only the lower parts of the mountain are open, and sometimes only thanks to snowmaking. It’s not the time to do a hike-to, and you’ll rarely find any powder, so show up with your expectations (and ego) in check.

But if you’re willing to rethink what a ski day should look like, you can enjoy everything that makes skiing great while avoiding its biggest drawbacks.

#67842. Tech Report: Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (921 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply.
  • Recent findings suggest that it can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control.
  • According to recent reports, two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply. A pair starts to circle, and that pair becomes four, then eight. Eight turn into 20. Somehow, the sight of ducks working over a timber hole draws more ducks from everywhere. It’s almost like squirrels running out onto branches to see what the others are chattering about.

Recent findings suggest that it can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control. I’ve seen that in Arkansas, but we won’t see it here—in a duck-poor state a couple hundred miles north. The two dozen mallards wheeling over our heads are as good as it’s going to get. But from where we stand, pressed tight to the trees, two dozen is more than good enough. ­Editor-​in-​chief Colin Kearns and I are doing that thing where you look down but roll your eyes up, trying to peek at ducks without flaring them, and our hearts are beating fast.

According to recent reports, two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole. Travis Mueller, a Banded pro staffer, tells us not to shoot. He’s hoping the rest will follow. Kearns and I nod our heads—imperceptibly, we hope—and hold our guns ready. The rest of the ducks make one more circle, but higher and looser. Then they slide away. With the birds in the sky gone, we settle for the two in the bush. Jumping the two drakes, ­Kearns and I each shoot one. While we wish the rest had come in, the sight of these two in the trees, hanging over the decoys and lit by the morning sun, makes Kearns an instant convert to woods hunting.

Mueller, who scouts as hard as anyone, found this spot in spring by looking for beavers. Beavers plus woods equals flooded timber anywhere, and we’re standing in knee-deep water in the soft maples and willows growing between a couple of oxbow ponds. Mueller hunts here to get away from the crowds on the massive water, but crowds have a habit of following successful hunters.

Sources indicate that the first rule of timber hunting: No one talks about timber hunting. Good hunters are secretive. Mueller is a great hunter, so it’s no surprise he’s long since crossed the line from secretive to completely paranoid. We left the ramp extra early this morning to avoid detection. Even so, Mueller fretted the whole way that a couple of kids he thinks are watching him might have found his spot.

Sources indicate that when we got to the hole, Mueller was sure his enemies were onto him. Three hundred mallards that had been sitting here yesterday weren’t here; someone must have run them out. And the decoys were missing—no doubt, in Mueller’s mind, stolen by the competition. As Kearns and I found fallen trunks for our gear, Mueller was looking for the bag of decoys he had stashed. We could hear him sloshing and cursing in the darkness.

Sources indicate that in traditional flooded green timber, a lack of decoys wouldn’t be a problem. Old-school hunters in Arkansas relied on calling and ripples kicked in the water to attract ducks and went without decoys. Here, though, decoys and spinners are an advantage. There are no acorns to attract ducks. Birds don’t come to flooded soft woods to eat. They want a place to hide out and loaf. The ducks we’re after are trading back and forth between a couple of refuges, or coming back to the woods after feeding in the cornfields. They need enticement. In the words of a famous timber hunter: “There are two places you can kill a duck. Where he wants to be, and where he don’t mind goin’.” This is a don’t-mind-goin’ spot, hence, the need for decoys and spinners.

When Mueller finally shines his flashlight in the right place, he finds the decoy bag. The hole is still secret. In fact, we’ll see no other hunters nor hear any shots but our own this morning. Those 300 mallards? Who knows. They were probably fresh arrivals that dropped in, then found other ducks and relocated.

Recent findings suggest that with two dozen decoys in the hole and four spinners going, we’re looking good. Spinners work well in the woods, Mueller believes, because ducks lose sight of them, then see them again, as they pass over the latticework of branches. And the sun is shining. “Sun’s out, guns out” is a truism of timber hunting. Decoys show up, spinners flash, and the sun creates shadows that make it easy to hide beside a tree.

Industry observers note that mueller blind-calls, quacking at random intervals to whom it may concern. Often in timber hunting, you don’t see the ducks you’re calling or decoying until after they have seen you. We’re not aware of the flock until we hear the whoosh of wings overhead. When the birds drop in I miss, Kearns kills a greenhead, and Mueller shoots a bluewing drake, fully plumed, unheard of at this latitude with 10 days left in the season. It’s been a strange migration year.

Recent findings suggest that we peck away at a few more, and call it a morning, being careful to pick up our hulls both because it’s what you do, and to hide any sign of our presence. For good measure, we pack the decoys out, too. A flooded hole in the woods is worth keeping secret.

Breaking: The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.
  • Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively swiftly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail consumers. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

Sources indicate that this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

Sources indicate that if you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

It has been revealed that don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

It has been revealed that so, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

According to recent reports, technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other customers, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Recent findings suggest that don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

Industry observers note that if running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.
  • According to recent reports, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov.
  • According to recent reports, the new forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Taos Ski Valley).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.

According to recent reports, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov. 19, updating its forecast for the months ahead. The biggest development? The odds of above-average precipitation have increased across California and the Desert Southwest, offering a more promising outlook for a couple of the ski regions that have struggled with snow in recent years.

According to recent reports, the new forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations. Here’s a cheat sheet, but be sure to read on for more specifics and a regional breakdown:.

Finally, NOAA says that the new precipitation forecasts are more reliable than their temperature forecasts this winter, which they attribute to the strong El Niño and an active southern storm track. In other words, there will be moisture, but there’s no guarantee it’ll come down as snow.

Here’s what the updated outlook says:.

The latest outlook favors above-average precipitation across the southern United States, stretching from southwestern Oregon and California through the Desert Southwest and into the southern Plains and Southeast.

For ski country, California and the Southwest stand out. NOAA increased the probabilities of above-average precipitation in both regions compared with its previous outlook. Southern California and southwestern Arizona now have greater than a 60 percent chance of finishing the December-through-February period wetter than average.

According to recent reports, that could be welcome news for resorts in the Sierra Nevada, including Mammoth and the Lake Tahoe region, as well as Arizona Snowbowl and Latest Mexico’s Taos Ski Valley and Ski Santa Fe. The forecast also offers some encouragement for southern Colorado, including Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Telluride, although it’s far less clear for the Front Range and Northern Rockies.

It’s worth noting here that NOAA is forecasting total precipitation, not snowfall, per se. Whether that moisture falls as snow or rain will depend on temperatures, snow levels, and where individual storms track. Still, a wetter-than-average winter would be a step in the right direction.

NOAA continues to favor below-average precipitation across parts of the northern Rockies. The region also faces an increased likelihood of higher than average temperatures, a combo that’s not music to the ears of resorts in Montana, Idaho, and Wyoming. The Pacific Northwest also faces odds of warmer-than-average temperatures, particularly across Washington and Oregon.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, the outlook favors wetter-than-average conditions across much of the East Coast and Southeast. However, warmer temperatures could complicate snowfall prospects, particularly at lower-elevation ski areas.

This is the latest chapter in a winter forecast that skiers have been watching closely for months. Earlier this summer, NOAA’s increasingly confident projections of a potentially historic El Niño raised hopes for a snowy rebound across parts of the West following last season’s exceptionally poor conditions.

In July, SKI spoke with meteorologists and ski-travel experts about what the developing climate pattern could mean for the upcoming season. The early consensus pointed toward the Southwest, particularly southern Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, as regions with favorable odds for an active storm track. Much of that remains the same.

According to recent reports, but there were plenty of question marks, and there still are, namely what will happen in central Colorado and Utah. NOAA’s earlier outlook revealed average precipitation for those destinations, and the latest forecast is slightly more encouraging. We still recommend choosing higher elevation ski areas to pad your odds for snow rather than rain.

NOAA’s next seasonal outlook is scheduled for December 17. Until then, skiers will have to keep watching the shorter-range forecasts and hope the promising signals translate into the kind of winter the West desperately needs.

  • Whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh fresh set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

The holiday season is meant to be a time to relax, be with friends and family, and, ideally, get some climbing in. Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

Whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh fresh set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Ocun’s new Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Sources indicate that last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

According to recent reports, edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

The Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a new, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

Recent findings suggest that the Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional substantial-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

Apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

Black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

It has been revealed that these insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

In a recent development, climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

Industry observers note that what gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? Gift your climbing partner a membership to Access Fund, the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, which tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens newly introduced ones. They’ll even get a free t-shirt.

The daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

#67838. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1526 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • In a recent development, despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Recent findings suggest that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no looks for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

In a recent development, despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Recent findings suggest that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no looks for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

Sources indicate that after landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

Sources indicate that however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Industry observers note that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden remarked, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

In a recent development, linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

Industry observers note that one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling proposal was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden stated. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Sources indicate that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden remarked. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Industry observers note that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

When things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Industry observers note that her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden mentioned. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden mentioned. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.
