#67797. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2347 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

In a recent development, I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

Industry observers note that on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

Recent findings suggest that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Industry observers note that packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and rapidly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

Sources indicate that as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

It has been revealed that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

According to recent reports, within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

In a recent development, alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

Sources indicate that the climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in massive walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

Sources indicate that when we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

Sources indicate that at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we rapidly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Sources indicate that alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

Recent findings suggest that 1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#67796. Industry News: The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (717 w)

Industry News: The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes.
  • Even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside.
  • In a recent development, the root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes. But athletes of all levels can suffer from them.

Even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside. The stronger a skier you are, the harder you can push your quads on the mountain, which means “you can find a way to make them sore, no matter your skiing level,” he explained.

In a recent development, the root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout. When you intensely and repeatedly load your quads, you create microscopic tears in the muscle fibers. That damage may sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: it’s one of the triggers that tells your body to strengthen that muscle, Spencer said.

Still, the side effects can be unpleasant. As with any bodily injury, the microtears trigger swelling, which increases the pain you feel after exercise and causes that sore sensation, Spencer explains. Officially known as delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), this feeling sets in after your workout ends and can peak as late as two to three days after. So if you feel fine boarding the shuttle at the end of a long ski day, but find yourself hobbling to the toilet the next morning, DOMS is probably the culprit.

The true cure for DOMS is time. “You really just gotta wait for those [microtears] to heal,” Spencer stated. But there’s also something you can do in the interim to ease your pain slightly: quad stretches.

According to recent reports, by gently stretching your quads after a hard day on the mountain, you can decrease the intensity of your soreness by flushing out some of the inflammation in your muscles, Spencer stated. It won’t be a cure-all, but it can help you move and feel better in the short term. Read on for the specific moves Spencer recommends.

You don’t need a ton of quad stretches to find relief. In fact, Spencer says two are enough. You’ve probably seen these stretches before, and while, sure, they’re not the most exciting, they are simple and effective.

Optional: Do this stretch in a hot tub. The heat may also help reduce feelings of soreness.

The above stretches can be sufficient to help reduce quad soreness, but if you’re looking for more, Spencer also suggests other recovery methods.

Recent findings suggest that spend a couple of minutes foam rolling your quads, including the front of your thigh (from the knee all the way up to the hip) and the sides to hit the vastus lateralis (basically where your IT band is). Similar to stretching, foam rolling can bring some relief to the quads by reducing swelling in the area.

Sources indicate that another option: hop on a stationary bike and gently cycle your legs for ten to 15 minutes. This easy movement can also reduce soreness by pumping out inflammation from your quads, Spencer mentioned. Just make sure to keep the resistance and your effort level low. “It’s not meant to be a workout,” he said.

Stretches can ease DOMS in the short term, but if you want to prevent intense soreness altogether, strengthening your quads is the ticket.

“If you just build a little strength going into the season, you’re going to be less sore,” Spencer said. And you’re also less likely to get injured, he added.

Exercises such as quad sets, wall sits, and really any squat variation like traditional squats, Bulgarian split squats, and single-leg squats can all strengthen the muscle group.

In a recent development, “The thing I hear all the time is the only way to get ready for skiing is by skiing, and that’s a total lie,” Spencer remarked. There’s a lot you can do both in the off-season and throughout the winter to prime your body for the demands of skiing, he said. In addition to quad-strengthening exercises, he recommends hamstring, glute, and core moves, plus jumping exercises that train your ability to react to the unexpected.

#67795. A Basset Hound Indicated Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

A Basset Hound Indicated Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Newly introduced York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • Industry observers note that the day prior, Becky demonstrated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Newly introduced York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

Industry observers note that the day prior, Becky demonstrated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

In a recent development, new York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

According to recent reports, but time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with plans to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

When the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

Sources indicate that finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

Industry observers note that “This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch remarked that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

According to recent reports, “It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch said. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so promptly.”.

The hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

Industry observers note that people with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, said there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

Industry observers note that “In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly indicates. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

In a recent development, wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he claims SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody rapidly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

He claims e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Urgency is particularly vital in these cases, Cooper says. Research shows that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper says, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

#67794. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Newly introduced York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good company.”.

Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Newly introduced York near the Gunks. Right now, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her big three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

When Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It has been revealed that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

Recent findings suggest that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very rapidly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

We got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

Industry observers note that so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Industry observers note that will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

It has been revealed that every time we got to a fresh belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

Sources indicate that none of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he mentioned it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never indicated it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a big light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Recent findings suggest that lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Fresh York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

Industry observers note that as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#67789. Breaking: Hike of the Week: Explore the Dramatic—and Threatened—Big Bend on This Desert Peak

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (698 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Hike of the Week: Explore the Dramatic—and Threatened—Big Bend on This Desert Peak

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that nine years later, Substantial Bend is still beautiful.
  • One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: kellyvandellen/Getty Images).

In a recent development, the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S. and Mexico, I was amazed not just at how beautiful it was, but how peaceful. The buff and black-streaked limestone walls soared 1,500 feet over the water, the afternoon sun streaming through the gap. The river was running low and slow, trickling over the mud and rocks, no more than knee deep. I rolled up my pant legs and waded into the water, toward that invisible line in the middle of the river that split two countries.

It has been revealed that nine years later, Substantial Bend is still beautiful. Covering an area bigger than Rhode Island, this stretch of West Texas desert is home to some of the state’s most moving scenery, from river canyons to rocky peaks, with animal and plant life to match. Hikers willing to put in the work on the area’s rugged trails may spot javelinas rooting in the undergrowth or nocturnal, raccoon-like ringtails climbing up the cliffs and trees of the Chisos Mountains; they’ll see prickly pear cactus and ocotillo, a spindly, Seussian shrub equipped with vicious spines, growing wild in the desert flats. (That border, however, may soon be far more concrete. Read on for more on that.).

One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak. At 7,825 feet, Emory is the highest point in Major Bend and the Chisos, and enjoys commanding views of the terrain for miles around. Getting there, however, takes some muscle: The rough, 9.7-mile hike to the top ascends singletrack and rock stairs through oak, piñon, and juniper forest before ending with a final, dramatic scramble to the peak’s exposed summit. November, when summer’s broiling temperatures finally cool down, is an ideal time to hike it. (Note: There is no water at all along the Emory Peak Trail, and the NPS suggests hikers carry at least one liter per person per hour.).

Sources indicate that the round trip takes about 6 to 8 hours, and you’ll want to leave some time to relax afterward. Santa Elena Canyon’s picnic area is an ideal spot for an early dinner, and cap off the night at the park’s free riverside hot springs. (Due to recent flood damage, reaching both of these highlights is currently harder than usual. The paved road between Cottonwood Campground and Santa Elena is closed at the time of writing; drivers with a true 4-wheel drive vehicle and high clearance can get there on Old Maverick Road. Due to another closure, getting to the hot springs requires a 4-mile round-trip, relatively flat hike along a gravel road. Consider it part of the adventure.).

Sources indicate that starting at the Chisos Basin Visitors Center, take the Laguna Meadows trail for about a third of a mile to a fork, where you’ll hang a left on the Pinnacles Trail. Follow it as it steadily climbs, traversing desert flats and rocky slopes with the sheer top of Emory looming in the background. After another 3.4 miles, the trail reaches a saddle below the top of the peak. Continue on the Emory Peak Trail for another 1.5 miles, then tackle a final, somewhat exposed 30-foot scramble to the top of the mountain and 360-degree views of the park below. Retrace your steps to the trailhead, or break up the hike by reserving one of the Pinnacles campsites ahead of your trip.

Industry observers note that in an 8-1 decision on November 9, the Supreme Court approved a request by the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall through Major Bend, ruling against plaintiffs who had argued that the barrier would decimate rare plant species and cut off migratory routes for animals, and that it risked damaging ancient rock art and Native heritage sites. In Santa Elena Canyon itself, the Department of Homeland Security prepares to install vehicle barriers and surveillance infrastructure and clear patrol roads through the area. Conservation groups and state officials like Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa say they’ll continue to push to end construction in the park.

#67783. Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1012 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).
  • For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.
  • According to recent reports, in interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).

For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.

According to recent reports, in interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route. Atop his list of concerns, however, was the deadly Khumbu Icefall, the site of avalanches and dangerous crumbling seracs. Every spring, Sherpa porters and guides must make dozens of trips through the crumbling glacier to ferry food, tents, and oxygen to higher camps.

“If you run 20 trips on Everest over the next 20 years and hire 15 to 20 Sherpas each year, you’re putting a lot of people’s lives in danger,” Ballinger told Outside in a 2023 interview. “We don’t feel that we can run an ethical expedition from the south side.”.

Recent findings suggest that ballinger’s company, Alpenglow Expeditions, led a handful of trips to Everest’s south side in the aughts. But starting in 2014, Alpenglow exclusively led Everest trips from the mountain’s northern side in Tibet, which is controlled by China.

According to recent reports, now, Ballinger is taking steps to return to Everest’s southern side. In a recent interview, he told Outside that his three-year strategy for Alpenglow is to lead trips up Everest from both Tibet and Nepal concurrently.

Sources indicate that “Even though we still think the north side of Everest is better for our clients, we are considering the south side as a backup,” Ballinger said. “And ultimately, we hope to be able to run trips on both sides of the mountain, provided we get the approvals that we expect.”.

Returning to Nepal gives Alpenglow a backup plan in case China closes the peak to climbers, Ballinger stated.

It has been revealed that climbers tackling Everest from the northern side of the China-Nepal border enjoy a few advantages, namely smaller crowds and a Base Camp accessible by vehicles. But the Chinese government’s repeated decision to close Everest with little warning has stymied expedition leaders. In 2008, China closed Everest just weeks before the climbing season to allow the Olympic torch relay to ascend the peak.

According to recent reports, since 2016, China has shuttered Everest five additional times. It closed the peak in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic, and kept Everest off-limits through the 2023 season. Ballinger returned the following year with an expedition to the top.

Sources indicate that “We had incredible seasons on Everest in 2024 and 2025, some of the best of my life,” Ballinger said. “It was uncrowded, we had great support from the Chinese, and it was totally open.”.

In 2026, Ballinger and other guides were preparing for another successful season on Everest’s north side when China abruptly canceled the season in early March. The decision came painfully late in the season. Expedition operators had already promised paychecks to guides and mountain workers. And climbers usually arrive at Base Camps in China and Nepal in mid-April.

Sources indicate that “We took the financial losses and did the right thing,” Ballinger said. “We paid our Sherpas and our guides and our workers who waited until the end. We ate that cost.”.

Sources indicate that ballinger said he then gave his climbing clients refunds or deferrals to the 2027 season. One-third accepted deferrals to 2027, while two-thirds booked with other outfitters in Nepal in 2026, he said. Alpenglow helped its clients find expeditions to join on Everest’s south side for the 2026 season.

According to recent reports, “Financially it’s not easy,” Ballinger stated. “It definitely sucks, but we want the best for our clients.”.

Operating in both Nepal and Tibet, however, would allow Alpenglow to shift clients from one side of the peak to the other in the instance of a closure.

It has been revealed that “Between 2007 and this year—that’s 20 seasons—we’ve had to cancel six times,” he noted. “In those years there’s a lot of stress.”.

Ballinger cited the rapid introduction of cargo-carrying drones on Everest’s south side as another reason for his decision to return. In 2026, a manufacturer called Airlift Technologies began ferrying gear and supplies from Base Camp at 17,500 feet over the Khumbu Icefall up to Camp I at 19,900 feet via heavy-duty cargo drones.

Alpenglow’s lead guide, Esteban “Topo” Mena, spent time at the Nepali Base Camp in 2026 to watch the business grow.

“We sent Topo to check out the scene and see if he thought the experimentation that’s going on with drone technology had a meaningful impact,” Ballinger said. “We think we can replace all of our Sherpa carries through the Khumbu Icefall with drones.”.

Each drone delivery to Camp I eliminates a human trip through the Khumbu Icefall. In 2026, several Everest outfitters relied heavily on Airlift Technologies’ drone service to transport gear above Base Camp.

The drone business grew out of two seasons of testing. Starting in 2024, Nepali drone companies began completing test flights of heavy-duty cargo drones amid the thin air at Everest Base Camp. In 2025, drone pilots successfully flew an oxygen canister and bags of gear from Base Camp to Camp I, proving the potential for a drone business.

The drone business is not without its problems. In 2026, the Nepali government grounded Airlift Technologies’ drones for four days without explanation.

Sources indicate that piloting a cargo drone over the Khumbu Icefall requires skill and technological innovation. One pilot at Base Camp controls the drone at takeoff. But when the craft reaches a specific elevation, a second pilot at Camp I takes over control, navigating the craft past towers of ice and sheer rock walls to land it on the upper flanks of the Khumbu Glacier.

“We see it as a really exciting change,” Ballinger remarked. “We’ve been talking for years now about what would allow the icefall to become manageable in the long term. We think drones are a stepping stone in that direction.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, snow on the mountains above Rollins Pass, Colorado. (Photo: SWKrullImaging via Getty).

A late fall hike turned into an overnight rescue on the Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail on November 14 when a trio of hikers called for a rescue after encountering severe weather and wintry conditions at 11,600 feet.

Sources indicate that located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet. When hiked in its entirety, it also involves 3,742 feet of elevation gain over the course of 18 miles. Recent day-time temperature highs in the area have hovered between 26 and 37 degrees, while lows were recorded at 5 and 9 degrees with wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

Grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR), which responded, said that the hikers called for help after encountering dangerous trail conditions, significant snow, and navigational struggles. The team dispatched a group of rescuers who rode ATVs up the Rollins Pass Road before dismounting and hiking the remaining distance there. When rescuers made it to the trio, they found the hikers were wet, cold, and tired.

“The subjects had set up camp but lacked appropriate gear, including fire making supplies, to spend the night in the deteriorating weather,” rescue officials wrote. A second rescue team joined the party later in the evening before accompanying the hikers back to the staged ATVs and from there to the trailhead.

Recent findings suggest that although most of Grand County has yet to see significant snow, November can be a deceptive time of the year to hike in Colorado’s high country. Trails may appear accessible, but factors like extreme temperatures, inclement weather and reduced daylight hours can make hiking and camping more treacherous than usual.

The Continental Divide Trail is the highest-elevation long trail in the United States, with its high point at the summit of 14,278-foot Grays Peak. Colorado’s section is the highest on the trail; the USFS estimates that the CDT’s average elevation across the state is 10,000 feet.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by Upcoming Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

Sources indicate that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Sources indicate that insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Fresh Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

It has been revealed that then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (298 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • According to recent reports, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

According to recent reports, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential concerns.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

#67768. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1638 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • Industry observers note that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more vital to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

Industry observers note that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy indicates. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up says, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

Industry observers note that 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

Industry observers note that 6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

According to recent reports, 7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

Recent findings suggest that for parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he notes. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

In a recent development, 9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

It has been revealed that 12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

Industry observers note that 13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

Recent findings suggest that 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a fresh way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

Sources indicate that 17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

Recent findings suggest that for activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

It has been revealed that 19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

It has been revealed that 20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s that time again.
  • According to recent reports, I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves.
  • If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

According to recent reports, I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

Industry observers note that 1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

According to recent reports, 2. Proposal a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

Industry observers note that 6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

Recent findings suggest that 7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

Industry observers note that 8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

In a recent development, 9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

It has been revealed that 11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

It has been revealed that 13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

Recent findings suggest that 15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

In a recent development, 16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

According to recent reports, 17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

According to recent reports, 18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

It has been revealed that 19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

Sources indicate that 20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

Sources indicate that 22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

According to recent reports, 23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

In a recent development, 25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

Industry observers note that 27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

In a recent development, 28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

According to recent reports, 32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

Sources indicate that 33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

Recent findings suggest that 35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

Sources indicate that 36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

Recent findings suggest that 37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

Sources indicate that 39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”.

40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them. Whether you resort to a countdown timer or go the “this is your last show” route, it’s pretty much always a struggle.

Sources indicate that perhaps you need a upcoming strategy. Parenting coach Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.

A few things to note about this method. Using language like “We have one more song” instead of “This is our last song before we leave for school” focuses on what the child is doing now versus what you are doing in the future. It’s easier for kids to accept the transition this way.

“Melodic intonation” is when you use a sing-songy voice to make a statement. It helps kids notice what you are saying and acknowledge it. Take a look at Miss Rachel and a lot of the other preschool-focused programming, and you’ll see it employed often. Using melodic intonation for the phrase “iPad is all done” helps to signal the transition for the child.

It’s key to remember that even when using a technique like this, it will take you doing it the same way over and over several times before your child catches on and gets with the program. If they have a meltdown, don’t engage; stay calm; and move on.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs). To keep them out of trouble and thoroughly entertained, we’ve rounded up some awesome games for toddlers that are sure to be a hit, whether you’re indoors or outdoors. The best part? Your kiddo won’t know it, but they offer ample opportunities for hands-on learning. Ready for endless fun? On your mark. Get set. Go find your tot’s new fave!

Toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning. Learning with play is essential for their development because it improves small and large motor skills, muscle strength, emotional intelligence, language development, spatial awareness, and more. According to an article by Michael Yogman, MD, FAAP, on Healthychildren.org, “research demonstrates play can improve children’s abilities to plan, organize, get along with others, and regulate emotions. In addition, play helps with language, math, and social skills, and even helps children cope with stress.”.

In a recent development, figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat. There are outdoor games, indoor games, toys, beginner board games… You get the idea. The key is to decide which activity is right for your kiddo, and that depends on factors like their age, energy level, developmental stage, and other milestones.

One of the most crucial things to consider is what interests your toddler. Do they love Ms. Rachel? Are they obsessed with a sport? Do they love baby dolls or animals? Once you figure out what will keep them interested, you can go from there.

Sources indicate that another factor is something called Play Schemas, a concept first used by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget. As stated in My Play Cupboard, Play Schemas are repeated patterns of behaviour you notice children engaging in when they play. Nine schemas can be commonly observed in young children, including connection, transforming, enveloping, enclosing, and positioning.

Once you figure out which Play Schema your toddler is drawn to, that will help you decide what type of games they’ll enjoy the most.

Industry observers note that give your jumping bean something to jump about—letters! We love that this outdoor game from The Imagination Tree combines alphabet awareness with the chance to get those wiggles out. Simply write letters in sidewalk chalk and have your little one hop from one to another as you call them out. And all you need to get started is a set of sidewalk chalk. Read all about it and check out the phonics and math variations over at The Imagination Tree.

In a recent development, let your toddler be your boss with a few rounds of Simon States. Toddlers love the chance to be in charge! Then, you can give the commands for a bit. It's silly, active, and engaging—that's why it's an early childhood classic. Plus, it gives little ones a chance to practice following instructions, taking turns, and building listening skills. Simon Says go play!

According to recent reports, toddlers love climbing under, over, and on top of all sorts of things. Obstacle courses let you take that natural climbing instinct and make it a game. Build an indoor obstacle course with painters' tape, making lines for your little one to walk on top of and jump over. Or take the fun outside and challenge them to stay off the grass in the yard or the wood chips at the playground. Ready for a bonus round? Turn the obstacle course game into follow-the-leader and take turns being the leader. Check out this post for even more obstacle course fun.

What are the benefits of toddler games?

Playing games with your toddler is not only a great opportunity to enjoy quality time with your child, but they help develop key life skills like problem solving, small and large motor skills, physical coordination, hand-eye coordination, and learning how to be social with others.

What types of games are best for toddlers?

In a recent development, while it depends on your child’s age, interests, and development, the best toddler games are simple and fun. Popular ideas include pretend play, memory games, music games, and basic movements, like a simplified version of Simon Claims.

How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers?

According to the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, toddlers should have very limited daily screen time.

It has been revealed that there are online toddler games that are designed specifically for young children. Parents should always review the game or content before allowing their child to watch, monitor usage, and opt for an ad-free, child-friendly tablet or platform.

What are some fun indoor games for toddlers?

Toddler indoor games should be fun and easy to set up: memory, obstacle courses, block building challenges, sensory stations, and pretend play like “the floor is lava,” “vet clinic,” and “grocery store.”.

If you're the type of parent who is pretty good at finding a million things that you feel like your child is going to love, especially during the holiday season, it can be helpful to think of the popular rule of four gifts that a lot of parents are trying to stick to in order to avoid not going overboard.

The rule of four can help parents keep their spending in check while also cutting down on an abundance of extra gifts that may not be used or fully appreciated. If you're looking to incorporate the rule of four gifts into your family's world this holiday season, it's actually really simple to follow. #67759. Latest Update: Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (828 w)
