Of course, we’ve all left the 1900s behind and have grown into adults — parents and women with careers.

Industry observers note that like the rest of us, the 52-year-old mom of two kids — Harper, 16, and Holt, 11 — has left high school in the rear view mirror, but her career continues to flourish. And she’s still in the classroom, in a way: Coven Academy, the witchy dark academia series in which she stars as the principal of Crescent Veil Academy, just got renewed for a second season.

You can also find her on Instagram, where her account is a delightful mix of food, fashion, humor, nostalgia, and life as a woman who is finding power and peace as she enters her 50s.

Sources indicate that recently, Thiessen partnered with Always on its “Period Talks Don’t Have to Be Scary” campaign, which addresses what is often a real hurdle for parents: talking about periods with their kids. Research has found that 43% of moms struggle to start the first-period talk because they feel unprepared. So Thiessen wants to share her own experiences while offering practical advice to parents who want to open and informative with their tweens and teens... even if can be awkward at times.

She recently sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about periods, parenting, her newly introduced show, and her family’s holiday traditions.

Scary Mommy: Gen Z and Millennial moms have done a lot to break period stigma with our kids. How have you done that with your kids?

Tiffani Amber Thiessen: I think the generation I grew up in didn’t talk about these things. Now kids are much more open, and I have a very open relationship with both my children. It never fully takes away the scariness of intimate talks, whether it’s periods, the body, or growing up. But I think parents who understand that it isn’t one big, intimidating conversation, but many small, casual talks, can take the edge off.

Sources indicate that partnering with Always has been lovely because they’re trying to prepare parents with what to do and how to have that first conversation. Being prepared gives you the confidence.

Sources indicate that SM: I found that I was a lot more scared than my daughter was. Did you feel that?

TAT: Most parents feel that way. You don’t realize until afterward that it really isn’t that scary. I found it to be a bonding moment. I’d tell my kids that over half the population menstruates, so it’s not a big deal. Keeping it casual and a little funny helps. Building that competence between parent and child is what lets your daughter take it on, and it’s a badge of honor.

SM: I love asking this: What’s your best piece of parenting advice?

According to recent reports, TAT: It goes back to having an open conversation about anything. When I became a parent, I wanted to be open to receiving anything my kids share, whether it’s hard or difficult. I wanted them to feel comfortable and know I would never judge. We’ve all been in crazy places, and my kids are super open with me, about the fun stuff and the stuff that isn’t so fun. Keeping that conversation free of judgment is probably the most key thing in parenting.

SM: Have you ever wanted to judge, though?

TAT: I can secretly judge, is that okay? [laughs].

In a recent development, TAT: Most of the things my kids tell me I’ve either witnessed, been through, or know someone who has. It’s really not that crazy.

Recent findings suggest that SM: Let’s switch gears to Coven Academy. And you just got renewed for Season 2?

TAT: Monday! We had high hopes and wanted to find an audience that saw the specialness of the show, and I think we did. It’s done very well on Disney+ and Hulu, so we’re over the moon to do it all over again.

SM: There are so few shows made for this demographic: tweens, mostly girls. It’s so good to have something that speaks to kids in that space.

In a recent development, TAT: The witch aspect is having a moment on social media, but it’s not really about spells and potions. It’s about found family, sisterhood, and having each other’s backs. I have a teenage daughter, and she has a wonderful group of girls she can count on. Everybody should have that, especially women.

SM: How has it been going from being a student on a hugely popular show to a headmistress on set with the younger generation?

In a recent development, TAT: It feels natural. I have kids of my own now. The last few indicates I’ve been fortunate to do have had younger casts, and I really enjoy working with young adults. I may give them advice, but I get a lot from them, too. We did a lot of night shoots, and I’d see these kids at 3 a.m. doing their TikToks while I was struggling. Their energy kept me going through those nights.

In a recent development, SM: The holidays are coming up. Do you have any family traditions you want to share?

TAT: We’re very traditional in that it’s all about family. We do Christmas morning and Christmas Eve dinner. For the last 15 or 16 years, we’ve alternated between my husband’s family in Texas and ours. This year it’s our turn to go to Texas. We leave the day after Christmas and spend the week and Newly introduced Year’s with my in-laws. All the cousins are together, and we look forward to it every year.

SM: What have you been cooking lately, or what are you planning for the holidays?

TAT: My kids like the traditions. Thanksgiving is classic turkey and stuffing, plus my mom’s famous cream cheese pie. For Christmas we usually do enchiladas, which I’ll probably make again this year. We usually switch it up for Christmas because everybody’s over turkey.

SM: Dennis Haskins recently passed away. He was your principal on Saved by the Bell, and now you’re playing a principal. Do you have any remembrances to share?

Industry observers note that TAT: I have so many. He was our solid one; our anchor. I know it was probably hard for him, being the only adult on a kids’ show. He handled it with such grace and gave us a safe place. He was part of us, and he could be young, but he was still a strong personality. He always made us feel protected, and he’s very much missed.

45 Years Ago, One Kids Book Series Taught A Generation How To Make Bad Decisions

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine if you could tell Bilbo Baggins to leave the ring behind for Gollum, have Leslie not swing on the rope to Terabithia on that rainy day, or remind Jonas to pack warmer clothes at the end of The Giver.
  • It has been revealed that for a generation, these interactive novels transported readers through space and time to form their own stories, putting them in the cockpit of planes, the gi of a judo master, or even the fins of a shark.
  • A few variations of the cover to “Sugarcane Island,” the first ever CYOA book.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choose Your Adventure for life.

Imagine if you could tell Bilbo Baggins to leave the ring behind for Gollum, have Leslie not swing on the rope to Terabithia on that rainy day, or remind Jonas to pack warmer clothes at the end of The Giver. Most fiction is concrete, with the authors dictating what happens next. But that changed when two writers figured out a way for the reader to control a character because the reader was that character. We’re talking about Choose Your Own Adventure, of course. The first published installment arrived in 1979, with The Cave of Time — though as we’ll see that wasn’t really the first book. For decades, Choose Your Own Adventure was an atypical experiment in literary determinism that resulted in one of the most-read book franchises ever created.

It has been revealed that for a generation, these interactive novels transported readers through space and time to form their own stories, putting them in the cockpit of planes, the gi of a judo master, or even the fins of a shark. By the end of the 90s, CYOA closed the chapter on its story, but nearly twenty-five years later, the tech giant is back in action. Here’s how it all began, ended, and began again.

A few variations of the cover to “Sugarcane Island,” the first ever CYOA book.

Interactive books weren’t a completely new idea before Choose Your Own Adventure (CYOA), but its predecessors weren’t mainstream popular. There was a romance novel from the 1930s, where the reader decides which suitor the protagonist marries, with dozens of possible endings. Several high-concept stories arrived by the 50s and 60s, like Raymond Queneau’s surreal Story As You Like It or Robert Coover’s explicit and unsettling The Babysitter. Celebrated for their uniqueness, none of these caught on beyond their novelty and were purely adult fare. It wasn’t until a lawyer teamed up with a young writer to find a way to bring this idea to bookshelves across the country.

Recent findings suggest that edward Packard came from a family deep in the legal business, but practicing law was never something he truly cared about. While his passion was writing, Ed’s children's books were never picked up by publishers. His fate changed one evening in 1969 while making up a bedtime story for his two daughters about a character named Pete. Struck by writer's block, Packard couldn’t figure out how to progress the tale and asked his kids what should happen next. When both girls answered differently, he realized Pete was never the protagonist – it was his kids living those adventures firsthand in their imaginations. Immediately, Packard knew he was onto something.

Industry observers note that ray Montgomery had just started Vermont Crossroads Press in 1970, after cutting his teeth writing roleplaying scenarios for Clark Abt, a pioneer in educational games. The Yale and NYU grad had aspirations larger than his employer and ventured out to make a name for himself in publishing. When Packard walked into his office with a draft of Sugarcane Island in 1976, Montgomery saw great potential that perfectly aligned with his interests. “I Xeroxed 50 copies of Ed’s manuscript and took it to a reading teacher in Stowe,” Montgomery stated in an interview from 1981. “His kids — third grade through junior high — couldn’t get enough of it.”.

Sugarcane Island became the best-selling book of the upstart publisher, moving over five thousand copies, but they were still an unknown entity in a crowded landscape.

According to recent reports, it was this point where things started to get messy for Packard and Montgomery. Both writers saw a potential for larger success beyond the small Vermont publishing house, and the two pursued greener pastures, independent from each other's ventures. Packard published two CYOA-style books in 1978 under the Harper imprint, Lippincott. Meanwhile, Montgomery’s agent managed to obtain a six-book deal from Bantam in 1979, and the two writers came together to officially launch the CYOA experience as we know it today.

Similar to the origin story of Sugarcane Island, Packard turned to his kids for story ideas. His daughter, Andrea, told him about her summer escapade, spelunking, and her desire to wander solo to explore more. She imagined a tunnel that could transport her to another time or place, and her dad loved it! Andrea scribbled more notes and ultimately ideated the first published CYOA book, “The Cave of Time.”.

Interior from “The Cave of Time” with two of the multiple endings available to readers.

While hiking through Snake Canyon, you come upon a cave you’ve never noticed before. You step inside and can potentially travel to medieval times, a prehistoric era, the Ming Dynasty, and other periods. Along the way, you can find your fortune through a foolish king, dine with cavemen, battle the Loch Ness Monster, try to escape the sinking Titanic, or any number of unpredictable possibilities. Some endings are bittersweet, others hopeful, and some are just plain grim.

Sources indicate that A fortuitous mistake resulted in Bantam overprinting this inaugural entry, and the publisher remedied its overstock by donating 100,000 books to schools and libraries throughout America. This charitable act guaranteed their target audience would have no problem discovering the book, transforming CYOA into a household name practically overnight.

50 books later, readers returned to the cave for another adventure, making it one of the few retro CYOA titles to have a sequel. For her efforts, Andrea received a credit in the book and a percentage of royalties that still come to her mailbox decades later.

Abandon all hope ye who turn the page!

Industry observers note that the opening page of every CYOA book warns readers they are responsible for their own fate. There’s no backtracking allowed (in theory), creating a flexible narrative where the outcome changes each time a page is turned. More often than not, the wrong turn leads to fatal consequences. But, really, who hasn’t flipped backward to reconsider a choice?

Few books offer the chance to be the master of a protagonist’s destiny, have wild adventures in a pocket-sized format, and combine those parts with the element of risk and uncertainty from a single decision. Some books have as many as 40 endings, and that finality could happen as early as the first ten pages. While most readers sought the happily ever after conclusion, others found pleasure in seeing how many ways they could fail in the grizzliest way possible.

It has been revealed that nope, this is definitely not going to end well. Don Hedin illustration from “The Forbidden Castle.”.

“My philosophy was that it should be like life,” Packard once said, with the intent of including moral realism in the reader's experience. Smart choices were typically better than impulsive, haphazard decisions, but morally virtuous ones weren’t guaranteed to be the wisest, and you often paid for heroics with self-sacrifice. Cheating was discouraged, but technically, if you didn’t take your finger off the page, it wasn’t a final decision.

It has been revealed that there was one time when being mischievous paid off, and that famous case was the twelfth book, Inside UFO 54-40. This is the only book in the series that explicitly rewards cheating. In order to find the secret alien planet, the reader must forego the typical CYOA patterns and stop playing along. Only by reading the book straight through would they stumble on a page unmarked by any choices to discover this paradise. “You did not make a choice, or follow any directions, but now, somehow, you are descending from space—approaching a great, glistening sphere.” The lesson was ambiguous, but a valuable one - sometimes, disobeying the rules is its own reward.

Stacks of CYOA books are common in any library or bookstore no matter where you live.

It has been revealed that CYOA books dominated stores around the world during the ’80s and ’90s, with hundreds of millions of books sold in 38 languages. But as the fresh millennium approached, Montgomery and Packard found themselves at a crossroads with no page to turn.

In a recent development, video games were taking over, as screen time replaced reading. Sales dwindled until the organization flew the white flag in 1998, ending with book #184, Mayday, which Packard co-wrote with the person responsible for the very first title in the franchise, his daughter Andrea.

In 2003, Montgomery and his wife Shannon Gilligan (who met while working on an Atari game based on the CYOA books) bought the rights to the franchise and revived it through Chooseco. Montgomery passed away in 2014, writing Gus vs. the Robot King, but Gilligan has kept the brand thriving as CEO while bringing it to newly introduced places.

Cover to Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School.

According to recent reports, today, CYOA sells an average of a million books annually, evolving to reach a more inclusive readership and touching on complications that affect modern society. Their bestseller remains a four-pack filled with Classics, but Chooseco transitioned into graphic novels like Eighth Grade Witch and offers longer CYOA books with titles like Time Travel Inn and Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School, which introduced their first nonbinary character. Readers ages 5 to 8 can dip their toes into the Dragonlark series, and even younger ones can start their adventure with the adorable board book The Abominable Snowman, with lethal endings absent from these kid-friendly editions. There are also board games, a math book, an upcoming Tarot card set, and a proposed book series for nostalgic adults with more mature themes — but nothing too explicit.

Packard wrote a trio of books in the CYOA style under the name U-Ventures in 2010 and continues to write fiction while maintaining his blog.

Montgomery always hoped the CYOA series would be a stealth reading program to excite kids into becoming voracious bookworms. Years later, his dream continues to be a reality and may soon rekindle that same love within adults who grew up on these books.

There are surprising aims beyond the traditional format that Gilligan couldn’t divulge in 2023, but even as technology evolves, nothing beats the experience of reading a physical book and not knowing what awaits the reader when they turn it over.

At Toy Fair 2023, Shannon Gilligan remarked: “Touching a page and moving it makes the brain think you’ve been somewhere on some super subtle level.” And even though she said Choose Your Own Adventure is at the “dawn of a relaunch,” the truth is, we’ve all been on this adventure for years.

According to recent reports, this article was originally published on Jan. 5, 2024.

Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.
  • Two fresh studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth.
  • Industry observers note that the studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Two fresh studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

Industry observers note that the studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

Sources indicate that the second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Recent findings suggest that both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

“Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

According to recent reports, parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

Sources indicate that according to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

According to recent reports, A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”.

It’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

This article was originally published on November 6, 2026.

Here Are The Rules To 19 'Bluey' Games Straight From The Show

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From “Keepy Uppy” to “Work,” and everything in between, here’s how to actually play Bluey games from the show with the whole family in real life.
  • In a recent development, raising kids is a daily learning experience, but Chili and Bandit make it look so easy in Bluey.
  • It has been revealed that we can’t all reach the same level of playtime excellence that Bluey’s Mom and Dad constantly achieve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From “Keepy Uppy” to “Work,” and everything in between, here’s how to actually play Bluey games from the show with the whole family in real life.

In a recent development, raising kids is a daily learning experience, but Chili and Bandit make it look so easy in Bluey. Sure, they have their tough times, like Bandit’s failed attempts at making a duck-shaped cake for Bingo’s birthday, or the Sticky Gecko incident with Chili (which she prefers we don’t talk about), but they overcome and make us want to excel at parenting as much as they seem to be. Much of that parenting and resolution comes from play — Bluey games that show good parenting and good fun can go hand in hand. Who knew animated anthropomorphic dogs would be our parenting inspiration, but here we are. But how do you play the games from Bluey in real life? What are the rules of the Bluey games?

It has been revealed that we can’t all reach the same level of playtime excellence that Bluey’s Mom and Dad constantly achieve. But you can recreate wonderful games. We’ve rewatched every episode of the show with attention to the games, and then we tried them at home with our kids. Did they all work as perfectly as they did on screen? Not exactly. But in general, did we have a good time? Are Pomeranians a hardy breed? Exactly. Here’s a list of 19 specific Bluey games that come straight from the show into your living room — a guaranteed good time for the whole family.

From Bluey Season 1, Episode 5, this game is best played in a wide-open field on a bright day with fluffy clouds looming in the sky. So, this one isn’t an everyday affair. Your kids hide under the shadows cast overhead, then run, jump, and scream into the next nearest shadow. Touching any part of the ground the sun hits means you’re out. It’s also a good way to stretch your budget on sunscreen.

Watch “Shadowlands,” on Disney+ here.

This game comes from Season 1, Episode 25, “Taxi.” Destination unknown, as your living room becomes a taxi, and your kid — the driver. Set up some chairs and a makeshift dashboard, and into traffic, you go! Watch out for pedestrians, other drivers, or whatever other hazards will get in the way of making your arrival on time. There are plenty of variations you can do with this game, changing the vehicle from a cab to a plane, train, starship, sandworm, or whatever imaginary vessel you want.

Watch “Taxi,” Bluey Season 1, Episode 25 on Disney+ here.

In a recent development, the game of “Raiders,” comes from Episode 16 in Season 1, which is called “Yoga Ball.” If you’ve got a Yoga ball in your home, you’re ready to play Raiders! The goal is to grab a lost treasure hidden behind obstacles you set up. Once they snatch it – you come after them and roll the ball down the hall to recreate that iconic movie scene. Really, though, if you’ve ever seen any Indiana Jones films, you can make up other gambits to chase your kids with. Even after the game ends, you can still teach them about monkey brains at dinner.

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 16, “Yoga Ball,” right here.

Industry observers note that I’d say who doesn’t love The Grannies on Bluey, but if your kids become half as exasperating as Janet and Rita, you will definitely have your hands full. This one comes from Bluey Season 1, Episode 28. The “rules” are simple: Your children dress up and act like octogenarians, turning mundane tasks into elderly-inspired chaos. If you’re daring, combine Grannies into any of the other games on this list, and watch the madness unfold.

Watch Bluey, Season 1, Episode 28, “Grannies,” right here.

Sources indicate that this game comes from Bluey Season 3, Episode 14, which is called “Perfect.” It’s a solid diversion if you’re at a gathering with other adults, but your children still want to play. Gently lob your kid in another direction and let them spin and twirl to their heart’s content. Then, like the game’s namesake, they return back to you, ready to be thrown again. Minimum effort on your part, but maximum fun for the little ones since they’re really the ones in control of how wild the boomerang is!

Watch Bluey, Season 3, Episode 14, “Perfect,” right here.

Recent findings suggest that from Bluey Season 2, Episode 3, it’s all about “Dance Mode.” Did your kids know there’s a switch on your back? If they find and flip it, you turn into a dancing machine – no matter where you are! If you’re coy, you can convince your children they also have a button that turns on their best jitterbug. This game is not for those who embarrass easily, but if you’re ready to show your kids how committed you are to playtime, Dance Mode turns everywhere you go into a boogie-down good time.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 3, “Dance Mode,” right here.

We all might think we know the game of charades, but Bluey Season 2, Episode 5, “Charades,” takes it up a notch. This is the only game on the list that requires investing a bit more into your game, but it’s worth it. Use a pack of Charades cards that don’t require reading and have pictures on them, then act out the image until someone guesses it correctly. It’s a lot of fun seeing how children interpret the world around them, you’ll be surprised how enjoyable this game can be with little ones. Nana Heeler plays this with the kids, so this is a good way to get grandparents or older relatives involved in playtime that won’t involve sprinting around the house.

Watch Bluey, Season 2, Episode 5, “Charades,” right here.

It has been revealed that from Bluey Season 2, Episode 14, “Fancy Restaurant,” we get a classic make-believe game with a new hilarious twist. Why go out for a dinner date with your significant other, when you can stay home and be served by your kids? They can be the maître d’, the waiter, the chef - or if they are feeling villainous, the lazy exterminator – and give you a night out you’ll never forget. I’d suggest setting some ground rules about what you’ll eat before you start playing. Otherwise, you’ll feel exactly like Bandit did at the end of that episode. Poor guy….

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 14, “Fancy Restaurant,” right here.

From Bluey, Season 2, Episode 3, “Bad Mood,” is sort of what it sounds like. Intended as an exercise in emotional regulation, the concept of the game makes it exceptionally fun for any situation. Bandit plays this with Bingo when she’s in a bad mood, climbing onto his feet and controlling her limbs as they smash into things, much to Bingo’s excitement. Even without a bad mood, your kids will love piloting a parent mech. Viking hats sold separately.

Watch Bluey, Season 2, Episode 3, “Bad Mood,” right there.

In Bluey Season 1, Episode 31, everyone gets down to business in “Work.” If you’re a remote worker, you already know the struggles of trying to stay afloat at the job while having kids scamper underfoot. The kids can interview you for a profession of their choice, and turn you into their employee to boss around. If you play your cards right, you might be able to distract them with the paperwork of their own to let you sneak in some actual work time. Try not to get fired - ideally from BOTH of your jobs!

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 31, “Work,” right here.

Industry observers note that in Bluey Season 1, Episode 36, everyone gets the travel bug with “Backpackers.” But, the trick here is nobody is actually going anywhere! Save money on a vacation to hike around the Alps or the Appalachian Trail, and instead backpack through Europe in your own home. Your children call the shots here, as they create the exotic locations and give you commands about what to do and say while on your excursion. Remember – as much as you wish you were, you are not a cartoon dog. Unless you’ve been doing your deadlifts, don’t wear the kids on your back if you want to be able to bend over when you’re older. What they can do instead is fill an actual backpack with household objects you’ll use on your trip instead of the items you’d actually need. Who needs a passport when you can hand Customs a toilet brush instead?

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 36, “Backpackers,” right here.

This one comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 10, “Rug Island.” Find the biggest rug or carpeted space in your home, drag some potted plants or couch cushions onto it, and transform your living room into a deserted island in the middle of the sea. Bluey and Bingo used felt markers to make all the objects in their little haven by the shore, but anything goes on the rug so take whatever you like and pretend it’s the essentials you need to survive. Imagination rules above all else, so immerse yourself in the mind of a child and drift away to simpler times when an island could just be a rug.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 10, “Rug Island,” right here.

This comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 2, “Feather Wand.” When Bingo discovered a feather on the ground, she quickly realized it was a magic wand. Whenever she pointed it at something or someone, she exclaimed “Heavy!”, and made it weigh a ton! You haven’t lived until you’ve cleaned your teeth with a floor toothbrush. Much of the fun happens when the objects are disenchanted, and suddenly become their original weight as they abruptly fly at your face once the struggle is over.

A variation on this would be from the episode “Magic Asparagus”, where your child transforms you into different animals by zapping you with an enchanted vegetable. Bluey used asparagus, but a sturdy carrot or parsnip would do the trick, too. Nothing leafy, unless you like cleaning up sprigs of supernatural broccoli from your dining room floor.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 2, “Feather Wand,” right here. Also, watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 49, “Asparagus,” right here.

According to recent reports, this game comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 25, “Double Babysitter.” A brilliant game to wear out your young ones, this game works best at night time when it's darker. Your child is the cat, trying to catch the “mouse” AKA the beam from your flashlight or laser pointer. Bluey and Bingo were elated to play this with their babysitter, and it will swiftly become a favorite with your little kittens, too.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 25, “Double Babysitter,” right here.

Industry observers note that not every game on this list requires the parents to break a sweat. I’m throwing you a bone here. This one comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 8, “Daddy Dropoff.” And, it’s a game you can easily play on your back in bed, while your kids have a romp with your frisky feet. Whatever is below your knees becomes the animal of your choosing, and your kids can play and take care of them. When you get tired of playing, just remind them of how stinky your feet are, and that should be enough to send them running.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 8, “Daddy Dropoff,” right here.

Industry observers note that as the day comes to a close and you are all winding down, Favorite Thing is a fantastic way to interact with your kids at mealtime that doesn’t wind them back up. This comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 7, “Favorite Thing.” The rules are simple: Everyone takes turns sharing what their favorite thing was that happened to them today, and you discuss it and turn their singular experience into a moment everyone enjoys. This a sneaky way to get your kids better at their conversational skills and having etiquette at the dining table, while also creating fun family memories that will last a long time after the plates are cleaned up.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 7, “Favorite Thing,” right here.

It has been revealed that this game comes from a classic Bluey episode: Season 1, Episode 8, “Fruit Bat.” It’s typical to read a book to your kids at bedtime to help them sleep, but it’s a bit unusual for you to fall asleep while reading their book. Try as you might, you just can’t stay awake, especially when you get to the exciting parts. Your kids can try to wake you up, but you’re having such a hard time keeping your eyes open! Whether you finish the book, or flop onto their pillow for a nap of your own, is up to you.

Watch Bluey, Season 1, Episode 8, “Fruit Bat,” right here.

According to recent reports, this comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 46, “Octopus.” Chloe the Dalmation learned this game from Bluey, who explained Dad is the octopus behind their couch, and the two kids are fish trying to steal his treasure. The octopus tries to stop them with his tentacles, swinging them at the fish and trapping them in his suction cups. Simple enough, and easy to play.

In a recent development, the dilemma is, when Chloe brings the game back to her home to play with her dad, it isn’t the same experience. Every time one suggests something, the other felt like their ideas were being rejected. Instead of turning the other person down, they decide to say yes to everything and remake the game to fit the way they play.

The lesson Chloe and her dad learned is when it comes to games, there are no rules. Playtime with your kids is like improv comedy. It’s best when it’s “Yes, and –“because saying no grinds the scene to a halt. There are still boundaries that must be respected, but let your imagination go as far as they can reach to make playtime a truly enjoyable experience for everyone involved.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 46, “Octopus,” right here.

Sources indicate that the game that started it all! From Bluey Season 1, Episode 3, this game is essential. Blow up a balloon, toss it to your tiny ones, and let the havoc begin. As long as the balloon never touches the ground or pops, the game continues! If it does land, throw it back in the air and start again.

Watch “Keepy Uppy,” on Disney+ here.

Sources indicate that this article was originally published on Jan. 13, 2023.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a kid-safe saw (yes, really) to a screen-free telephone “club,” these are the picks blowing up our mom group chats.

According to recent reports, it happens like clockwork every fall: Our mom group chats turn into one long stream of links. “Is your kid asking for this, too?” “Is it sold out??” “Ordering now; better safe than sorry!” IYKYK, and if you’re behind, well, we’ve got you.

Our editors pooled our mom group chats to parse through all the convos and conjecture about what our kids want this year, and we came up with a list of kids’ gifts real moms are actually buying (or have already procured and stuffed in a secret hiding place). There’s the landline for kids that you’ve surely been seeing all over your social media feeds, a play saw that won’t cut little fingers, a balance board that’s sneaky good for everyone in the house, and much more. There’s guaranteed to be something for every kind of kid on this list.

Keep scrolling for the gifts every mom we know is talking about.

For the baby or toddler on your holiday list, a Lovevery Play Kit is genuinely one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each kit is developmentally designed by experts for a specific age and stage, so every single toy inside has a real purpose and actually supports what that child’s brain is working on right now. The Free Spirit Kit is designed for older toddlers exploring independence, creativity, and imaginative play, and it comes with everything from open-ended building materials to pretend play pieces that grow with them well beyond the holiday season. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

The Sticki Rolls capsule series has absolutely taken over my daughter’s friend group, so she will lose her mind when she sees Series 3 under the tree. Each roll is a peel-and-stick experience that reveals collectible band stickers inside, and the trading, collecting, and comparing with friends has become a whole social event in itself. They are the kind of small, inexpensive gift that delivers an enormous reaction, which is the ideal holiday gift math. It’s the perfect stocking stuffer or add-on for any kid who is deep in the sticker and collectible era right now! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that this is the holiday gift that every parent who is trying to delay handing their kid a smartphone needs to know about. The Tin Can is a Wi-Fi landline designed specifically for kids, with no screen, no apps, no social media, no browser, and no strangers getting through. You control the approved contact list from the app, kids can call friends and family with real voice calls, and there is even a free Can-to-Can proposal so two Tin Can kids can call each other for free with no subscription required. My daughter loves it and I love that she gets the independence of being able to call her people without me handing over the entire internet to do it. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that this is such an ideal holiday toy for me! It's physical but can be done inside, it's not made of plastic, it doesn't have noise or lights, and... I can use it too after the kids go to bed. Also you don't have to wrap it. Really, can you ask for anything more? — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

The Melissa & Doug Cheery Lane House is the kind of gift that becomes the centerpiece of playtime for years — it is a beautifully detailed wooden dollhouse play set with colorful, cheerful design that sparks hours of open-ended storytelling and creative play without a single battery or screen required. Melissa & Doug has been the gold standard in wooden toys and imaginative play for decades, and this set delivers on every bit of that quality and craftsmanship. — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that the Noodoll Ricespud Hot Potato is a tiny, perfectly rendered little potato plush that is so absurd and so cute at the same time that it is genuinely impossible not to love it. It is soft, squishy, palm-sized, and has the most deadpan little potato face that somehow communicates everything. It’s the kind of completely unhinged gift that costs almost nothing, takes up zero space in a stocking, and becomes the most talked-about thing under the tree because nobody expected a potato and yet here we all are. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, the ChompSaw is the coolest thing I have seen for kids who want to actually make things. It is a real, functional saw designed specifically for children with a safety guard that prevents the blade from cutting skin but still cuts wood, foam, and cardboard perfectly, which means she gets the genuine satisfaction of building and creating without me hovering anxiously over every cut. It’s designed for kids 4 and up, requires zero power tools or adult intervention once they gets the hang of it, and the independent building projects it unlocks are genuinely impressive. — Katie Garrity.

I love this toy because it combines two really common kid interests: building things and dinosaurs. I got this set for my twin neice and nephew and they have gotten so much (QUIET, SOLO) play time from this set. This set allows you to make three different dinosauts — T-rex, pterodactyl, brontosaurus — and they make them over and over again. It's hands-on and it uses their brains, I couldn't ask for more. — Sarah Aswell.

My daughter has been asking to learn to sew and this is the perfect place to start. The Hug is a beginner-friendly kids’ sewing machine that uses yarn instead of thread, making it safe, easy, and genuinely manageable for little hands without the frustration of rethreading a needle every five minutes. It has a built-in safety finger guard, LED lighting, and comes with a full sewing kit so she can start creating immediately right out of the box. — Katie Garrity.

I have a soccer obsessed kid; specifically, he wants to play goalie all the time. We practice every. Single. Day. And he always wants more time and more kicks to block. This soccer launcher has been so fun. It will fire on a five-second timer or if you clap three times, and you can adjust the height it debuts at too. It's a great "massive" gift for the soccer loving kid in your life. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

K-Pop and cool fashion dolls in the same box is basically a guaranteed win. The K-Pop Demon Hunters 3-pack features three fully styled dolls with incredible detail in their outfits, accessories, and overall aesthetic that feels genuinely fresh and different from anything else in the doll aisle right now. Each doll has her own distinct look and personality, and the whole set comes with the kind of intricate styling details that a kid who loves fashion, music, and K-Pop culture will absolutely obsess over. — Katie Garrity.

Magnetic tiles are one of those gifts that never get old, and a 132-piece set is the kind of haul that opens up a whole latest level of what they can build. The Sunny Auntie tiles are compatible with other major magnetic tile brands so they can add to an existing collection, the pieces are thick, sturdy, and safe with rounded edges and no sharp corners, and the variety of shapes in the set means endless architectural possibilities from simple towers to elaborate castles and everything in between. — Katie Garrity.

This collab between Melissa & Doug and the iconic Van Leeuwen Ice Cream is the most delightful play set, and the little ones on your holiday list are going to absolutely love it! It is a fully detailed pretend play ice cream counter inspired by Van Leeuwen’s gorgeous aesthetic, complete with scoopable play ice cream, cones, toppings, and all the tools needed for the most imaginative scoop shop experience. — Katie Garrity.

If you have been anywhere near a toy store, a bookstore, or the internet in the last year you already know that Jellycat has completely taken over, and this little Scottie Dog in his cozy winter jumper is exactly why. The softness is genuinely unmatched, the details are ridiculously charming, and every single Jellycat somehow manages to have more personality than a stuffed animal has any right to. My daughter because she has been asking for a Jellycat, and a dog in a tiny Christmas sweater felt like the obvious and correct choice. — Katie Garrity.

My 8-year-old niece loved this pen creation station. Craft kits feel like they're back in a significant way this year, and I love that this one is fun during the making and leaves you with usable pens she can take to school, and a fun little storage locker for her desk in her room. It's just little girl gift gold. — Katie McPherson.

In a recent development, knuffle Bunny is a full cultural moment right now, and if your kid has read Mo Willems’ beloved picture book series, getting the actual official stuffed animal is going to completely send them. The Gund version is beautifully made with that signature floppy, scrappy, well-loved look that matches the book illustrations perfectly, and the softness is exactly what you want from a toy that is going to become a forever comfort companion. — Katie Garrity.

The combination of Bluey and the Scribble Scrubbie concept is genuinely my daughter’s two favorite hobbies all in one. The Scribble Scrubbie pets are washable toy figures that kids can color with markers, scrub clean, and color all over again, which means the creative play never runs out. The Bluey version gives you Bluey and Bingo to color and decorate, which is going to be an absolutely unhinged amount of fun for any kid obsessed with the show. — Katie Garrity.

For the kid who already has a Nugget and is completely obsessed with Minecraft, this cover set is going to make the holidays. The Minecraft collab brings the iconic blocky aesthetic to the covers in a way that is genuinely cool and immediately recognizable to any fan. It transforms an already beloved piece of furniture into the ultimate Minecraft hangout zone without any new hardware required, just swap the covers and watch your kid completely lose their mind. — Katie Garrity.

We've tried a few different audio players over the years and the Yoto is the one that has really stuck for my son. He uses it every night to listen to a story while he drifts off, and he looks forward to the Yoto Daily podcast with Jake too. This generation of Yoto has so many features I love, from the built-in night light (no more traveling with both!), to the new green button on the side that makes it easy to toggle through favorite stories without carrying along their cards. This is a fabulous gift idea that'll truly be used and loved for many years to come (ours has been THROWN many times during toddler tantrums and still works like a dream). — Katie McPherson.

Industry observers note that this is a craft kit and a fidget toy in one, which is basically the dream combo for a kid who can’t sit still. The kit comes with 101 scented squishy beads in flower, heart, round, and star shapes, plus five reusable elastic bracelets and a beading needle, so my daughter can make a bracelet, squish it, take it apart, and start over. It’s a screen-free gift that keeps her hands busy for hours, and I’m not above admitting I’ll probably end up making a bracelet too! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that these are just the cutest overalls that remind me of what I wore when I was a kid. They're designed by Sergio Hudson, who did a special collaboration with Osh Kosh this winter. I love the pop of color, I love the stripes, I love it all. And I know your kid will, too. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

This is the gift that keeps my daughter happily occupied without a screen in sight, and the starter set means there’s no scrambling to figure out what else you need. You just set a Tonie character on top of the box and it plays stories, songs, and adventures, and it’s simple enough that she runs the whole thing herself. It’s become part of our daily routine, and it’s the kind of present kids keep reaching for long after the wrapping paper is gone! — Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that the “more is more” customizing trend is real in our house, and these let my daughter decorate everything she owns without a single bottle of glue. Each pack has 15 glossy, 3D resin charms in pink kawaii creatures, sweet treats, and whimsical icons that peel off the backing and stick to anything flat, like her phone case, journal, or water bottle. It’s a small, inexpensive gift that gets a major reaction, and I fully expect to find a tiny charm stuck to something I own by January. — Katie Garrity.

This new set from Magna-Tiles takes everything my daughter loves about building with Magna-Tiles and adds ball runs, which means she gets to engineer a track and then immediately test whether it works. The set has 78 magnetic pieces plus two racing balls, including a trapdoor, a slide, and curved and short rails, so she can build multi-level raceways with tight turns and major drops. It works with any Magna-Tiles she already owns, and it’s a screen-free gift that teaches cause and effect while she thinks she’s just playing. — Katie Garrity.

There’s SNOW much to love about this limited-edition Snoopy purse, which is designed to look like a mini puffer coat with a quilted detail and a chain strap. It comes in a pretty Swiss blue, closes with a magnetic snap, and is part of Janie and Jack’s winter PEANUTS collection, so it’s guaranteed to make her whole cozy-weather outfit feel complete. It’s small and special enough to fit all her tiny treasures! — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that I've had my eye on the Nex for a long time, and I wish I'd gotten one sooner! We love gaming as a family and it makes me so happy to have the Nex on the mantle for rainy or cold days when it's zero fun to be outside, but we neeeeed to move around and burn energy. It's gaming with way less guilt and feels like a family activity we all look forward to. And yeah, Fruit Ninja is just way more fun when you're karate chopping with your whole chest rather than getting finger burn swiping like crazy. — Katie McPherson.

It has been revealed that I got this set for my newly introduced niece, and I still cannot get over how perfect it is! It’s soft and airy, thanks to the 100% cotton gauze, and that hand-drawn tulip print? Stahhhp, it’s so charming. It’s a good thing my kids are no longer little or I would literally be buying up every single thing on this site. I think this would make the sweetest gift for any little girl in your life. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

In a recent development, this new board game has everything I like: easy rules, really beautiful design, and short game play (around a half-hour). I also love 2-player games that I can either play with one kid or with my partner. The premise is very simple: build a 3D volcano with certain features before your opponent does. I love that this can be very simple or very strategic — there's also an expansion set that bring the game up to 4 players. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that for the little racer who’s obsessed with Mario Kart, this officially licensed slot car set brings the game to the living room floor, with Mario and Yoshi going head to head on a 9-foot track with a built-in lap counter to crown the winner. It’s made for kids ages 3 and up and gives two players a screen-free way to duke it out, which is the kind of gift that gets pulled out over and over. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, if you have a kid who refuses to come inside until her fingers are numb, this is the snowsuit that lets her stay out there, because it’s waterproof and breathable, so she stays dry whether she’s sledding, skiing, or face-planting into a snowbank. It’s built with real snowsport details, including several pockets and adjustability, so it can keep up with a growing kid through the whole winter. It's a splurge, but it’s the one piece of winter gear that makes getting her out the door a lot less of a battle. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that anyone else have a Grinch-obsessed child? The Grinch with a light-up heart is basically the holiday plush equivalent of a happy ending, and she already quotes the movie every December. It’s an 18-inch, soft and fuzzy Grinch with a glowing heart on his chest, which makes it a great cuddle buddy and a night-time companion all season. Made for ages 2 and up, it’s the kind of gift that instantly becomes a holiday tradition (and gets a spot on the couch until Newly introduced Year’s). — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that now, this a video game I can say yes to without a second thought, with Bluey and Bingo finding Dad’s old camera and snapping photos around the show’s famous spots, then saving everything in a scrapbook she can decorate with stickers. It has local co-op so a second player can join in and strike a pose, plus no in-game purchases and no online play, which is the kind of kid-friendly setup parents love. The Deluxe Edition adds the Here Come the Grannies bonus content, extra dress-up items, and a digital art book, and the “For Real Life” activity ideas even get her playing away from the screen. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that OK so... I want one of these, too. My two tween girls are VERY into fidget toys and squishies, so we have a lot in my house. My favorite one to steal is this butter block. It's adorable on my desk and great to squeeze during meetings and phone calls. But also great for the kids they're meant for. And fits in a stocking! — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that for the toddler in your life who already knows every word to Ms. Rachel’s songs, this Yoto card puts the whole debut album on a screen-free player, with all 23 tracks, including “Icky Sticky Bubblegum,” “I Love a Rainbow,” “Substantial Feelings,” and a few classics like “The Wheels on the Bus.” Kids just pop the card into a Yoto Player or Yoto Mini to hear it, which means a dance party can happen without anyone handing over a phone. It’s $14.99, made for ages 1 and up, and the card introduces Nov. 12, so it’s available to preorder now, which makes it a perfect stocking stuffer for any family that already has a Yoto. — Katie Garrity.

For the kid on your list who’s obsessed with Star Wars, this 13-inch remote control walker is basically a movie scene they can drive around the living room, with a Mandalorian and Grogu figure riding in the cockpit. It really walks, runs, and turns with a 2.4 GHz remote, and it comes loaded with LED lights, laser cannon sounds, and real Star Wars audio clips, so every trip across the floor feels like a battle. It’s made for ages 8 and up and is a Walmart exclusive, and honestly the walker looks cool enough on a shelf that parents will be tempted to play too. — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, my 11-year-old kid is so hard to buy presents for. She's kind of not into toys anymore, but she's not ready to go over to the realm of all clothes and self-care and novels yet. Well... when I saw this Chia Pet bison... I know that she would have at least one thing under the tree that she absolutely loved. I love that this has a bit of a "toy" feel, but it's also cool room decor. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that these 14-inch dolls are incredily cute and well-made. I love that the dolls look like actual normal girls without exaggerated or sexualized features and I love that the price point adds a good option for families that can't drop three digits for an American Girl Dolls. There are also lots of great accessories available, also at reasonable prices! — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that I genuinely would put these on and wear them myself if I could, but I suppose I’ll just have to settle for watching my niece romp around in them. I love that these are fully waterpoof but also lightweight and flexible enough that kids don’t feel like they’re walking around wearing cinder blocks. Another great feature is the grippy outsole to help keep little ones from slipping while they’re exploring on wet ground. And they’re made from natural rubber, so totally non-toxic! — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, clickeez are tiny character keycaps that click and clack like a real mechanical keyboard, and the Series 3 Bubble Pops theme has a softer, quieter click that’s almost as satisfying as the surprise of seeing which ones you get. The Mega Pack comes with a keyboard-shaped case and 12 characters to display and swap in and out, plus there are 70+ characters to hunt for, including rare surprises, so she can build a collection one click at a time. It’s made for ages 6 and up and is a great screen-free gift for any kid who loves to collect (and click)! — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that the details in this LEGO build are amazing, from the chain-driven V* engine compressor to the functional steering and suspension. Honestly, I got this car for my (grown, adult) brother and a different, simpler Fast and Furious car for my nephew to build along side him. I love how many brain-building, screenless hours of fun these sets provide — and then you can watch the movie after. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that I mean, the title really explains everything. This shoots farts at people. I fully admit that I bought this for my brother's children and not for mine, and they played with it for *hours*. There was so much laughter, and honestly, the smell is not that bad for the adults in the room (although we did kick them outside). I think they ran more than when they play sports. — Sarah Aswell.

Is there anything cuter than a denim jacket on a child? No there is not. Enter this adorable teddy fleece-lined jacket that you just know your kid will love. It's cozy, classic and totally show-stopping. — Kate Auletta.

Every mom knows that it’s the absolute worst when your little one is feeling under the weather... and it can especially wreak havoc on sleep. This special Gund bear helps kids fall asleep by doubling as a sound machine with nine gentle modes. It even comes with a bedtime story! It’s created to kind of perfectly fit against a little one’s chest as they bring it in for a, well, bear hug, and that squeeze activates the soothing sounds. Kids will love getting it as a gift, but Mom might love it even more. — Julie Sprankles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bluey is the most beloved show on the planet. But you can’t see all the original versions in the United States.

Bluey has become not only the biggest kids’ show on the planet but one of the most popular TV series worldwide. Period. First airing in its homeland of Australia in 2018, the realistic portrayals of parenting combined with the zany wholesome hijinks of a pair of adorable animal sisters means the show is loved equally by kids and adults.

But. Not every single moment of Bluey is available in the United States. A handful of episodes were eliminated by American censors and/or Disney. Some episodes have also been heavily censored and/or altered for American audiences. Why would a kids’ show be censored or have episodes banned? It’s a reasonable question and the easy answer is: it’s complicated. Sometimes it’s because a word has a different connotation in the U.S. than it does in Australia. Other times, there’s an innuendo, or topic U.S. censors have deemed inappropriate.

Across all seasons of Bluey, references to Australian-specific things were localized for American audiences, so we won’t spend too much time discussing those unless they were explicitly censored for serious implications (as serious as Bluey can be, anyway). Likewise, certain bits of dialogue were altered through the series for various reasons, and unless it was something provocative, this article will also glance past those changes.

So, without further ado, here’s a full list of censored and banned Bluey episodes as of May 2023, including one very recent body-shaming moment in Australia.

According to recent reports, enhancement! This list now includes 2024 Disney+ versions of Season 3 episodes!

The good info about the first season is right now no episodes are banned in the U.S. anymore. However, a few notable changes were made to them, some of which were censored and altered outside of Australia.

According to recent reports, what was censored and why? A fairly wholesome and hilarious episode, this episode and two others from the first season, “Shaun” and “Teasing,” along with “Flat Pack” from Season 2 were censored due to the use of a racially-insensitive term that could refer to Aboriginal people. The ABC apologized and claimed it was not intended to refer to that abhorrent use of that word. “Daddy Robot” and the other episodes now use a nonsense word to replace the derogatory phrase.

Update: “Teasing” was restored on Disney+ when Bluey season 3B was added, replacing the offensive phrase with “Shoobi-doo-wop”.

What was censored and why? A scene where Bluey is playing “Penguins” in the bathroom was cut from the U.K. and the U.S., although it’s still referenced in the episode. The cut scene has Bluey sliding around the room, something that could be dangerous for a kid to do on a wet tiled floor.

In a recent development, what was it censored and why? The episode ends in the U.S. with Bandit finally boarding his imaginary airplane, only to realize the reckless cab driver is also his pilot. However, the original version continues after that realization, with Bingo’s character pretending to throw up on Bandit’s lap. In the U.S. version, there is no vomit, and that’s why the episode ends earlier here than in the original one.

Recent findings suggest that what was censored and why? As the girls are looking for a way to use some cash, they meet a unicorn handler (actually a pony with a horn on her head). Bluey is excited at this idea but learns only one of them can have a ride on her. Their disappointment swiftly disappears after the unicorn drops a huge turd on the grass, leaving the kids fleeing as they scream their heads off. The turd does not exist in the Disney+ version.

Industry observers note that this horse and her owner were seen again in the Season 3 episode “Pass the Parcel,” only this time the horse had already relieved itself. In the original version, her feces can be seen in a wide shot where the kids are playing the game, but the American version has an alternate version with the poo pile missing.

In a recent development, what was censored and why? At one point in the episode, Bingo asks her dad how babies get into mom’s bellies. This line is cut in the U.S. version. Apparently, Disney doesn’t want pregnancy discussed in-depth in a show aimed at preschoolers.

The second season brought a few upcoming challenges to the show that needed resolutions, including one episode that will probably remain in the Disney vault until the end of time.

Why was it banned? Similar to “Daddy Putdown,” this one is even more focused on pregnancy and carrying babies. The episode does not exist on Disney+ and in the U.S. at all. In it, Bandit (the dad) simulates what it’s like to give birth. The entire episode is banned as a result.

Will it be unbanned? Most likely never. Unlike “Family Meeting” (aka “the fart episode”) it appears this one is not coming to Disney+ anytime soon.

Sources indicate that why was it changed? Jack seems to act like a child with ADHD. Although he is too young to comprehend the way his brain understands the world around him, he knows it works differently from others.

In the original version, Jack tells Rusty “There’s something wrong with me.” It was later revised to “There’s something going on with me.”.

Why was it censored? Bluey hands Conductor Bandit something when he asks for her ticket that she instructs him to rub all over his face. In the original version, imaginary poop was passed to her dad. In America, the line was changed to transform that invisible heap into a slug.

Why was it censored? We already discussed earlier how this one was hit with the same racially-insensitive insult heard in “Daddy Robot,” but there may be another reason this one was controversial.

Recent findings suggest that the core of this episode is a whirlwind examination of the cycle of life, rife with metaphors and silliness to keep it light. However, this episode does include a part that can be interpreted as an afterlife, and it’s also possible to see this plot as a baby’s first look at evolution.

Presently, the episode is available on all platforms in the U.S. with only the derogatory term removed. If you haven’t seen it in a while, it’s a deeply moving six minutes worthy of a rewatch.

According to recent reports, the release of this season has been split into several batches of episodes. At the time of publication, Australia is about to get the third part of the season, with no intends on when it will come to the United States.

What was censored? The episode opens with Bandit looking unhappy about the results of weighing himself, grabbing his sides remorsefully. Chilli shows similar dissatisfaction when she does the same. Arguably one of the biggest chunks to be edited out of this show, “Exercise” turned into a huge divisive battle immediately with accusations of fat-shaming, and concerns centered around body dysmorphia in children and adults. Ultimately, the first minute of this episode was removed across all global distributors due to these concerns, instead starting in the backyard with Bandit beginning his workout routine and no discussion on the shape of his body. To be clear, this episode has not even aired yet in the US.

It has been revealed that why was it censored? In one flashback, Bandit is playing “Boomerang” with Bluey while having a conversation with Fido. In the original version, the conversation seems to be about getting neutered, or in human terms having a vasectomy. When it arrived in the U.S., it was changed to be about having Bandit’s dog teeth removed.

Sources indicate that why was it censored? In a scene where Bingo and Bluey teach Bandit how to use a swing, the girls intentionally position him so it hits him in the crotch, causing him to cry out, “My groin!” That word is eliminated in the U.S. version.

Also in S3, the word “groin” is edited out of the U.S. version of “Chores” when Bandit complains about hurting his groin after attempting to do Bingo’s “Bee-yoop” silly walk.

Why was it censored? When Bingo proves to Bluey she’s annoying too, only in a different way, the younger sister tapes her nose back and puts fake teeth into her mouth. Bluey indicates she looks “crazy” in the Australian version. The word “crazy” does not appear in the U.S. version.

As opposed to an abrupt cut to hide something like Bandit’s groin hit in “Born Yesterday,” the cut is not noticeable at all and adds to the element of surprise once Bingo reveals herself.

Why was it censored? While having an imaginary drive with Bluey that starts to take a turn into madness, her stuffed cat Agatha threatens to pee on the curtains. In the censored version, Agatha instead tells them she’ll scratch their curtains.

Industry observers note that what was censored? When Muffin goes on a rampage and tries to escape from her dad while still on the call, she runs around the house, eventually smashing into the bathroom, which Trixie is using. In the original version, Trixie can be clearly seen on the toilet, forced to cover herself up. The American edit crops this out, instead keeps the shot tight on Muffin’s face so as not to reveal the scene behind her.

Upgrade: As of the summer of 2023, “Faceytalk” has been restored to the original version, with Trixie easily seen seated in the bathroom.

In a recent development, why was it censored? Unicorse is using his best moves to get on Chilli’s good side in the worst way possible. While showing off his sweet moves, Chilli remarks about the chili sauce stain on his body. Australians heard Unicorse respond with, “Wanna’ lick?” The American version has altered this to “Want a bit?”.

Why was it censored? Twice in “The Decider,” the two families of sports fans tease each other by saying their team will “flog” the opponents. A term more commonly used with Australian sports fans than Americans, Disney+ viewers will instead hear “beat” due to the violent implications of what the other word means.

Why was it banned? The obvious reason is the sheer volume of references to passing gas. There isn’t any real potty humor here, but the impetus of the episode is based around a silent but deadly affront to poor Bluey’s nose.

Recent findings suggest that why was it banned? In the opening moments of "Relax," Bandit calls the kids "Super Troopers" in the US edit. However, in the original Australian version, he refers to his girls as "Dingle Berries." What's so controversial about a nonsense word? Turns out the phrase has more than one meaning, and while many know it as a way to insult someone's intelligence, it stems from something more fecal. Apparently, when it comes to Disney Plus, bathroom humor and Bluey mix like cereal and windshield washer fluid, so those berries were better left where they belonged.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking to find all the episodes closer to how they looked when they initially aired, the only way is to get the DVD of Season 1 and Season 2, which is region-specific to the United States. There are also other ways to find Bluey episodes, but even the hardiest of Pomeranians wouldn’t dare look in those dark corners of the web. Occasionally, the ban does lift on an episode, but so far, that’s only happened once or twice.

Non-banned Bluey episodes air on Disney+ in the United States.
